m1-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Create a Colab notebook that saves to your Google Drive, and connect the notebook to Drive so files you write survive a restart.
  • Build a project folder where raw data, code, and results each have one obvious home.
  • Record your Python and library versions in environment.json and pin them in requirements.txt.
  • Detect, months later, whether your environment has drifted from the one that produced a result.

In October you train a model on your science fair data and it scores 0.91. In January a judge asks you to rerun it with one extra feature. Before you change anything, you rerun the old version to have a starting point, and it scores 0.84.

Which number is real? You can only answer if you know four things about the October run: which data file it read, which code it ran, which library versions it used, and which random seed it started from. Most student projects can't answer any of the four, and the published literature isn't much better. This module sets up all four on the first day, so every result you produce in this course can be traced and rerun.

#What you need

  • A Google account. A personal one is the reliable choice. Some school accounts block Colab or Drive access for apps, and you only find out when a cell fails.
  • A browser on any computer. Chromebooks work fine.
  • No installs. Colab runs Python on a Google virtual machine. It normally ships with NumPy, pandas, SciPy, statsmodels, scikit-learn, and matplotlib, which are the six libraries this course uses. The version cell below confirms that for your machine.

If you'd rather use Jupyter on your own computer, the optional section near the end covers it.

#Create the notebook and connect it to Drive

  1. Open colab.research.google.com (opens in a new tab) and sign in.
  2. Choose File › New notebook in Drive.
  3. Click the name at the top left (something like Untitled3.ipynb) and rename it 00-setup.ipynb.
  4. Run a first cell with Shift+Enter to connect to a runtime.

The notebook file itself lives in your Drive's Colab Notebooks folder. Files your code writes are a different story. By default they land on the virtual machine's disk under /content, and that disk is erased whenever Colab recycles your runtime. A result saved there is gone by tomorrow. Connect Drive so your project folder is permanent:

Colab asks you to approve access in a pop-up. Afterwards, your Drive appears at /content/drive/MyDrive, and you can also browse it from the folder icon in the left sidebar (the same panel has a Mount Drive button that does this for you).

#Lay out the project so raw data stays raw

A research project produces three kinds of files: data you were given or measured, code you wrote, and things the code produced. The most useful rule in computational research is to keep them apart and never edit the first kind by hand. If you fix a typo directly in your raw spreadsheet, nobody (including you in three months) can tell which values were measured and which were corrected.

This cell builds that layout. In Colab, point PROJECT at your Drive (the comment shows how); here it's a relative path so the cell runs anywhere.

exist_ok=True makes the cell safe to rerun: running it a second time changes nothing instead of crashing on folders that already exist. The README check works the same way, so rerunning never overwrites notes you've added. results/runs will hold one small record per experiment, which you'll start writing in the next lesson.

#Record the versions that produced your results

Library updates change results. Default hyperparameters change between releases, random number streams get reworked, and a deprecated argument starts raising an error. To rerun an old result you need the versions it ran on, so write them down at the start of every project.

That output came from the machine that built this page. Colab will print Linux for the operating system and may show different version numbers; that's expected. What matters is that the numbers are written into the project next to the results they produced.

importlib.metadata.version reads the installed package's version without importing it, and it uses the name you'd type after pip install, which is why the list says scikit-learn rather than sklearn.

#Pin the versions in requirements.txt

environment.json is a record for humans. requirements.txt is the same information in the format pip reads, so someone else can rebuild your environment with one command.

The == is the point. A line that says scikit-learn installs whatever is newest on the day someone runs it, which might be three releases after yours. A line that says scikit-learn==1.8.0 installs the version you actually used. In Colab, someone rebuilding your environment would run this in a cell, then choose Runtime › Restart session so the newly installed versions are the ones Python loads:

#Check for drift when you come back

When you reopen a project weeks later, compare the current environment with the record before trusting any rerun. This cell is worth keeping at the top of every analysis notebook.

Here it matches because the record was written a minute ago. On a fresh Colab runtime next semester it may not, and then you'll know that a changed score could come from the libraries rather than your code.

🧪 Try it yourself

Edit the record to fake an old version, then rerun the drift check: add recorded["numpy"] = "1.26.4" as the second line of that cell. The check should name NumPy and both versions.

A local setup has no session limits and works offline. Make a virtual environment inside the project folder so its packages stay separate from everything else on your computer.

On a Chromebook, Colab is the simplest route. With the Linux development environment turned on, or on any Linux computer:

Once a project has a requirements.txt, replace the long install line with python -m pip install -r requirements.txt, which installs exactly the pinned versions.

#Problems people hit on day one

drive.mount fails or the pop-up says access is blocked. Your school account doesn't allow Drive access for Colab. Switch to a personal Google account from the profile picture at the top right and create the notebook there.

FileNotFoundError for a file you saved yesterday. Either the file was written under /content instead of your Drive (so it was erased with the runtime), or Drive isn't mounted in the current session. Run the mount cell first, then check the path starts with /content/drive/MyDrive.

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'statsmodels' on your own computer. The virtual environment isn't active in that terminal, so Jupyter is using a different Python. Activate it (your prompt starts with (.venv)), then start jupyter lab again.

PackageNotFoundError: scikit-learn from the version cell. The package isn't installed in this environment at all. Install it, and in Colab restart the session afterwards.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Your notebook saves a results table to /content/results.csv. The next morning the file is gone, but the notebook is still in Drive. What happened?

  • The notebook lives in Drive, but /content belongs to the virtual machine. Save under /content/drive/MyDrive after mounting.

  • There's no such rule; everything on the runtime's disk goes when the machine does, whatever the file type.

  • The notebook saved fine. The CSV was never in Drive in the first place.

Show answer

A. The notebook lives in Drive, but /content belongs to the virtual machine. Save under /content/drive/MyDrive after mounting.

2Why pin scikit-learn==1.8.0 instead of writing just scikit-learn in requirements.txt?

  • pip accepts a bare name; it just installs the newest release.

  • Pinning reproduces the environment that produced your numbers, not today's.

  • Speed is about the same. The benefit is that everyone gets the same version.

Show answer

B. Pinning reproduces the environment that produced your numbers, not today's.

3You find a typo in a value in data/raw/plants.csv. What's the reproducible fix?

  • Then nobody can tell measured values from corrected ones, and the original is lost.

  • The correction is now documented, repeatable, and reversible, and the raw measurement survives.

  • Silently dropping data changes the results and hides a decision a reader should see.

Show answer

B. The correction is now documented, repeatable, and reversible, and the raw measurement survives.

Key takeaways

  • Mount Drive and keep the project under /content/drive/MyDrive; files under /content alone are erased with the runtime.
  • Separate data/raw (never edited), code, data/processed, and results, so every derived file can be regenerated.
  • Write library versions to environment.json and pin them with == in requirements.txt on day one.
  • Compare the current environment with the record before trusting a rerun of an old result.

#Further reading

  • A Quick Guide to Organizing Computational Biology Projects (opens in a new tab) by William Noble: the short, classic paper behind the "raw data stays raw" layout, with a lab-notebook habit you'll use in Lesson 3.
  • Good enough practices in scientific computing (opens in a new tab): a practical checklist for data, code, and project organization written for researchers who aren't software engineers.
  • Colab FAQ (opens in a new tab): Google's answers on runtime lifetimes, idle timeouts, and where files are stored.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain what a random seed does and why NumPy's default_rng(seed) is the form to use.
  • Generate a dataset from a seed, save it to data/raw, and fingerprint the file with SHA-256.
  • Estimate a treatment effect with a confidence interval using statsmodels.
  • Write a run record (seed, data hash, versions, results) and prove a rerun matches it exactly.
  • Run a smoke test that touches every library in the course.

Here is a tiny simulated experiment: 24 control plants, 24 fertilized plants, and the fertilizer adds about 2 cm of growth. The cell runs it twice and prints the estimated effect each time.

Same code, two different answers, and if you run this page's code yourself you'll get two more. Neither number is wrong. They're both honest draws from the same process. The problem is that you can't write either one in a report, because nobody (you included) can regenerate it. A seed fixes that.

#How a seed replays the same "random" numbers

A random number generator is a deterministic machine. It holds a hidden state, and each draw transforms that state into a number and a new state. The seed sets the starting state, so the same seed always produces the same sequence. Step through this program and watch first and second fill up.

The second random.seed(7) rewinds the generator to the same starting state, so the second list is a copy of the first. For NumPy, use rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) and draw from rng everywhere. The older np.random.seed(...) sets one global generator that any library can silently advance, so a seed set at the top of a notebook doesn't protect a cell that runs after some other code has drawn from it.

#Step 1: Simulate a greenhouse experiment from a seed

Real experiments have structure, so this simulation does too. There are three greenhouse benches with slightly different light, 16 pots per bench, and the fertilizer is assigned at random within each bench (8 fertilized, 8 control), which keeps bench light from piling up in one group. The true fertilizer effect is built in as 2.0 cm.

Every random choice in the function, both the treatment shuffle and the measurement noise, comes from the one rng built from seed. That's what makes the whole dataset a function of a single integer.

#Step 2: Fingerprint the raw file

A file name tells you nothing about a file's contents. greenhouse.csv in March and greenhouse.csv in May may differ by one edited cell. A cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 turns the file's bytes into a 64-character fingerprint, and changing even one character changes the fingerprint completely.

Store the hash with every result. If a rerun reads a file with a different hash, you know the data changed before you start hunting for bugs in the code.

#Step 3: Estimate the effect and plot the data

Look at the data before you model it. Each dot is one pot.

Now estimate the fertilizer effect while accounting for the benches. C(bench) tells statsmodels to treat bench as a category, so each bench gets its own baseline height and the treatment effect is estimated within benches.

We built a true effect of 2.0 cm into the simulation, and the estimate from seed 42 is about half that. That isn't a bug. With 24 pots per group and 2.5 cm of plant-to-plant noise, an estimate this far off happens, and the confidence interval is wide enough to say so. Notice that 2.0 sits inside the interval.

#Step 4: Write a run record

A run record is a small JSON file holding everything needed to regenerate and recognize a result.

#Step 5: Prove the whole run repeats

The real test is to rebuild everything from the seed (data, hash, fit, record) and compare it with the saved record.

rerun == saved compares every key and value, including the data hash, so True means the data and the result are the same down to the fourth decimal. The second part is just as useful. Running the identical experiment with 20 other seeds shows how much the estimate moves from sampling noise alone, about 0.6 cm here. Keep that idea in mind: a difference between two models or two conditions that is smaller than the seed-to-seed spread isn't evidence of anything yet.

#Smoke test: every library in one cell

The last check confirms that SciPy and scikit-learn work too, using the same data.

The low R² is the honest answer, not a failure: bench and treatment explain only a small part of the plant-to-plant variation, which is mostly noise. If you see Toolkit works, your setup is ready.

#When the rerun doesn't match

rerun matches run-001: False after editing nothing. Something drew random numbers outside rng. Look for np.random.normal(...), random.random(), or a scikit-learn object without random_state; each one uses a different, unseeded generator.

The hash changes but the numbers look identical. The bytes differ even if the values don't. A different pandas version can format floats differently, and opening and resaving a CSV in a spreadsheet program can change line endings or quoting. That's exactly why raw files are written once and never resaved by hand.

The record compares as False because of a timestamp. If you add the time a run started (useful), leave that key out when you compare records.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1You call np.random.seed(0) in the first cell, then run cells out of order and get a different result than yesterday. Why?

  • The seed fixes the start of the sequence, not where your cell lands in it. A local rng = np.random.default_rng(0) passed to your code avoids this.

  • A seed is just an integer; it doesn't expire. The generator's position in its sequence is what changed.

  • Seeds work the same on every machine.

Show answer

A. The seed fixes the start of the sequence, not where your cell lands in it. A local rng = np.random.default_rng(0) passed to your code avoids this.

2The seed-42 run estimated an effect of about 1 cm, but the simulation's true effect is 2 cm. What's the right conclusion?

  • With 24 pots per group and 2.5 cm of noise, estimates vary by roughly 0.6 cm between seeds, so 1 cm is unlucky but plausible.

  • One dataset gives one estimate. The interval and the 20-seed spread both show how far off a single run can be.

  • Picking the seed that gives the answer you want is cherry-picking, and in real research you don't know the true value.

Show answer

B. One dataset gives one estimate. The interval and the 20-seed spread both show how far off a single run can be.

3Two run records have identical results but different data_sha256 values. What does that tell you?

  • SHA-256 is deterministic: the same bytes always give the same hash.

  • Maybe it's only formatting, maybe it's an edited value. The hash tells you to check before trusting either result.

  • The function is the same each time; different hashes mean different input bytes.

Show answer

B. Maybe it's only formatting, maybe it's an edited value. The hash tells you to check before trusting either result.

Key takeaways

  • A seed sets a generator's starting state; create one rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) and draw everything from it.
  • Fingerprint raw data with SHA-256 so you can tell when a file has changed.
  • Save a run record (seed, data hash, versions, model, results) next to every result.
  • Prove reproducibility by rebuilding from the seed and comparing with the record, and measure how much results move between seeds.

#Further reading

  • NumPy random Generator (opens in a new tab): the official guide to default_rng and why it replaced the global np.random functions.
  • Ten Simple Rules for Reproducible Computational Research (opens in a new tab): rule 6 is about recording random seeds, and the other nine are worth the ten minutes.
  • hashlib (opens in a new tab): Python's hashing module, including hashlib.file_digest for hashing large files without loading them into memory.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Keep a dated research log that records what you tried, why, and what happened.
  • Use Runtime › Restart session and run all as the test a notebook must pass before you trust or share it.
  • De-identify a table about people and know when a science fair needs review before you collect data.
  • Draw charts that stay readable for color-blind readers.
  • Turn a confusing error into a minimal reproducible example.

In February you dropped 31 plants from your dataset because their labels were smudged. In April your mentor asks why the sample size in your poster is 31 smaller than the number in your proposal. If the reason lives only in your memory, the honest answer is "I think there was a reason." Research is full of small decisions like that one, and a project is only as trustworthy as its record of them.

#Keep a research log next to the code

A research log is a plain text file in the project folder with one dated entry per working session. Each entry answers four questions: what you did, why, what happened, and what's next. It takes two minutes at the end of a session and saves hours when you write the report.

Notice what the second entry captures: a number changed, and the log says why it changed. That's the entry that answers your mentor's question in April. Keep negative results too. "Tried a random forest, no better than linear" is a finding, and it stops you from trying the same thing again in May.

#A notebook isn't finished until it survives Restart and run all

A notebook keeps variables in memory between cells, so the order you ran cells in, including cells you've since deleted, shapes what's in memory. A result can depend on a cell that no longer exists. Before you trust a number, put it in your log, or send the notebook to anyone, choose Runtime › Restart session and run all. If every cell runs top to bottom and produces the same numbers, the notebook is a real record. If it crashes halfway, you've found a hidden dependency while it's still cheap to fix.

A few habits make that test easy to pass:

  • Number notebooks by stage: 01-audit.ipynb, 02-baseline.ipynb, 03-model.ipynb. Each one reads files written by earlier stages instead of relying on variables from another notebook.
  • Put the drift check from Lesson 1 in the first cell, and set SEED once near the top.
  • Move a function to src/ once you've copied it into a second notebook, so there's one version of it.

Colab also keeps history for you. File › Revision history lists saved versions of the notebook you can restore, and File › Download › Download .ipynb gives you a copy to keep with the project or put under version control.

#Protect the people (and places) in your data

If your project uses data about people, such as surveys, health measurements, or anything with names, ages, or locations, privacy rules apply before any code does. Science fairs that follow the ISEF rules require an Institutional Review Board (IRB) to review and approve student research with human participants before any recruitment or data collection. Projects that use only preexisting, publicly available datasets, with no interaction with people, are generally exempt from that preapproval. Check the human participants rules (opens in a new tab) and your fair's own guidance early, because review takes weeks.

Even with approval, keep identifying details out of the files you analyze and share. This cell de-identifies a small survey table: it drops names, swaps student IDs for random codes, and coarsens birth dates to years.

The key table that links codes back to students is the sensitive part. Keep it out of the project folder and out of anything you share or upload, and delete it when the study no longer needs it. This is also the one place in the course where a seed would be a mistake: anyone who knew the seed could regenerate the codes.

⚠️ Watch out

Shared notebooks leak data in their outputs. A notebook whose last run printed survey.head() still contains those names after you delete the cell's code, because the output is saved in the file. Before sharing, choose Edit › Clear all outputs, then restart and run all on the de-identified data only. Don't paste private data into public forums or AI chat tools either.

Locations can be sensitive too. Field biologists routinely blur or withhold the coordinates of rare species, because a precise location in a public dataset can lead collectors or poachers straight to them. Round coordinates or publish them at a coarse grid when that risk exists.

#Draw charts everyone can read

About one in twelve men has some form of color-vision deficiency, and red versus green is the pair most often confused. Two cheap fixes cover most cases: use a color-blind-safe palette, and make groups differ by marker shape or line style as well as color, so the chart still works printed in greyscale.

Labelling each line directly also removes the legend, so readers don't have to match colors across the chart. For your own comfort while working, Colab's settings (the gear icon at the top right) include a dark theme and a larger editor font size.

#Getting unstuck: read the last line, then shrink the problem

Here's an error you'll meet in some form this year. The CSV came from a spreadsheet, and the column clearly says height_cm.

Read a traceback from the bottom. The last line, KeyError: 'height_cm', says pandas has no column with exactly that name; everything above it is pandas' internal route to that conclusion. When a name "obviously exists" but isn't found, print the exact names as a list, where the quotes make invisible characters such as spaces visible:

The spreadsheet left a trailing space in the header: 'height_cm '. Stripping whitespace from every column name fixes it.

When you can't find the cause yourself, build a minimal reproducible example before asking anyone. Copy the failing line into a fresh cell, replace your dataset with three or four rows typed inline (like csv_text above), and delete everything that isn't needed to trigger the error. Half the time the bug becomes obvious while you shrink it. The other half, you have a ten-line example that a mentor or a forum can answer in minutes, and it contains none of your private data.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Your notebook gives a clean result, but Restart session and run all crashes at cell 9 with a NameError. What does that tell you?

  • The restart is the reliable part: it shows exactly what the notebook's code produces from scratch.

  • The notebook as written can't produce that result. Fix the dependency, then recheck the number.

  • A typo would fail every time. Failing only after a restart points to hidden state.

Show answer

B. The notebook as written can't produce that result. Fix the dependency, then recheck the number.

2You share a de-identified table plus the notebook that made it. Which mistake can still expose participants?

  • Outputs are stored inside the .ipynb file. Clear all outputs and rerun on the de-identified data before sharing.

  • Random codes with the key stored separately are the recommended approach.

  • Coarsening to year reduces identifiability; it's one of the standard steps.

Show answer

A. Outputs are stored inside the .ipynb file. Clear all outputs and rerun on the de-identified data before sharing.

3A KeyError: 'temp_c' appears, but you can see a temp_c column in the spreadsheet. What's the fastest first check?

  • The library is fine; it's reporting a real mismatch in names.

  • Quoted names reveal 'temp_c ' or 'Temp_C' immediately.

  • The file name has nothing to do with the column names inside it.

Show answer

B. Quoted names reveal 'temp_c ' or 'Temp_C' immediately.

Key takeaways

  • Keep a dated research log: what you did, why, the result, and what's next. Record decisions that change numbers.
  • A notebook result counts only after Restart session and run all reproduces it.
  • Data about people needs approval before collection at ISEF-affiliated fairs; share only de-identified data, with the key stored elsewhere, and clear outputs first.
  • Make charts readable without color: safe palette, distinct markers or line styles, direct labels.
  • Read tracebacks from the last line up, and shrink a stubborn bug to a few inline rows before asking for help.

#Further reading

  • How to create a Minimal, Reproducible Example (opens in a new tab): Stack Overflow's guide to the kind of question that gets answered quickly.
  • The Turing Way (opens in a new tab): a free, community-written handbook on reproducible, ethical, and collaborative research, with chapters on data privacy and project design.
  • ISEF human participants rules (opens in a new tab): what needs IRB review, what's exempt, and the forms involved.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Rewrite a vague research idea as a question with a population, inputs, a comparison, an outcome metric, and a threshold fixed in advance.
  • Explain why a model that predicts well can still give the wrong answer to a "what causes this?" question.
  • Read a paper's claims, data, baselines, metrics, and effect sizes, and compute the uncertainty a paper left out.
  • Search Google Scholar, PubMed, and arXiv precisely enough to find the papers that matter.

"Can machine learning help farmers use less fertilizer?" sounds like a research question. Try to test it and it falls apart. Which farmers? Help compared with what, a soil test or guessing? Measured how, and how much less counts as success? Any result at all can be read as a yes, which means the question can't be wrong, which means it can't be tested.

Here's a version that can fail: "For wheat plots in one region's 2025 season, does a model using drone images of leaf color predict nitrogen deficiency at week 6 with recall of at least 0.80, compared with 0.65 for the standard handheld chlorophyll meter, on plots from farms the model never saw?" It's longer and less exciting, and it's the only one of the two you could put in a lab notebook and check in September.

#The five parts of a testable question

Medical researchers use a checklist called PICO (population, intervention, comparison, outcome) to pin questions down. For ML research it helps to add a fifth part: a success threshold written before you see results.

The comparison is the part students skip most, and it's the part reviewers check first. "Our model gets 0.91 AUC" means nothing until you know what a soil test, an existing model, or a one-line rule would get on the same plots. The threshold matters because it stops you from deciding what counts as good after you've seen the number you got.

#Prediction and explanation are different questions

Some questions ask what will happen: will this plot be deficient, will this patient be readmitted? Others ask what would happen if we changed something: does more fertilizer raise yield, and by how much? The first kind is prediction; the second is explanation, or causal inference. A model can be excellent at one and useless for the other.

This simulation makes the difference concrete. Each of 400 field plots has a soil nitrogen level, a fertilizer amount, a leaf greenness reading, and a yield. The rules are built in, so we know the truth: fertilizer raises yield by 0.02 t/ha per kg, greenness has no effect on yield at all (it's a symptom of nitrogen, not a cause of yield), and, as on real farms, farmers put more fertilizer on poorer soil.

First, the prediction question: can greenness alone predict yield on plots the model hasn't seen?

Greenness explains about half the variation in yield on held-out plots. As a predictor it's genuinely useful. As a lever it's worthless: painting the leaves green wouldn't add a gram of wheat, because greenness and yield are both downstream of nitrogen.

Now the explanation question: what does fertilizer do to yield?

The naive regression says fertilizer does nothing, with a confidence interval tightly around zero. That's confidently wrong. Poorer soils get more fertilizer, so the fertilizer's benefit is cancelled out by the soil's deficit in the raw comparison. Soil nitrogen is a confounder: it affects both the treatment and the outcome. Adjusting for it recovers the true 0.02. In real data you rarely know every confounder, which is why the strongest way to answer an explanation question is a randomized experiment, the topic of Module 3.

⚠️ Watch out

The classic mistake: reading feature importance as cause. A model's most important feature is the one that helps it predict, which may be a symptom, a proxy, or a measurement artifact. "The model relies on greenness" is a statement about the model. "Greenness affects yield" is a claim about the world, and the model can't support it.

#Read a paper like a referee

When you read an ML paper in your field, go past the abstract and answer five questions. Write the answers in a table; you'll build one in the next lesson.

  1. Claim. What exactly is claimed, about which population, and is it a prediction claim or a causal one?
  2. Data. Where did the data come from? How many independent units (patients, farms, sites), not just rows or images? How was the test set kept apart, by random rows or by new sites and later dates?
  3. Baselines. What does the model beat? A majority-class guess, the existing method, and a simple linear model on the same features are the minimum.
  4. Metrics. Does the metric match the use? Was it chosen before the results?
  5. Effect size and uncertainty. How big is the improvement, and how sure can we be? A paper that reports a single number without an interval leaves you to compute one.

These questions aren't academic. When Sayash Kapoor and Arvind Narayanan re-examined political science papers claiming that complex models (random forests, AdaBoost) predicted civil war onset far better than logistic regression, they found the advantage came from data leakage; once it was fixed, the complex models did no substantively better. Their running list of reviews (opens in a new tab) documenting ML errors in science, when this course was written, covered 41 reviews in 30 fields that together found problems in 648 papers.

Question 5 is one you can often answer yourself with one line of code. Suppose a paper reports 92% accuracy on a test set of 50 images, and another reports 92% on 1,000.

Same headline number, very different evidence. With 50 test images, the true accuracy could plausibly be anywhere from about 81% to 97%, so a claimed improvement from 89% to 92% is well inside the noise. The Wilson interval is a standard choice for proportions and behaves better than the textbook "plus or minus 1.96 standard errors" when the accuracy is near 100% or the test set is small.

#Find the papers that matter

Start broad, then narrow. Three free search engines cover most of what you'll need:

  • Google Scholar (opens in a new tab) covers every field. Put exact phrases in quotes, use the author: operator, and use the year filter in the left sidebar. Cited by shows newer papers that cite a result (often including critiques), and All versions frequently leads to a free PDF.
  • PubMed (opens in a new tab) indexes biomedical and life-science journals. Boolean operators must be uppercase, and field tags restrict where words appear: [tiab] for title or abstract, [dp] for publication date.
  • arXiv (opens in a new tab) holds preprints in ML, physics, math, and quantitative biology. Papers are moderated but not peer reviewed, so the five questions above matter even more.

Once you find one good paper, follow its references backward and its Cited by list forward. Two or three rounds of that usually surface the key papers in a niche faster than more keyword searches would.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1Which question is testable as written?

  • No population, comparison, metric, or threshold, so no result could show it's false.

  • "Accurate" compared with what, on which data, by which metric?

  • It names the population (held-out farms), comparison, metric, and a threshold fixed in advance, so it can come out no.

Show answer

C. It names the population (held-out farms), comparison, metric, and a threshold fixed in advance, so it can come out no.

2In the simulation, yield_t ~ fertilizer_kg gave an effect near zero with a narrow interval. Why was it wrong?

  • 400 plots is plenty; the interval was narrow. The problem is bias, not noise.

  • Soil nitrogen is a confounder. Adjusting for it, or randomizing fertilizer, recovers the real effect.

  • The same method gave the right answer once the confounder was included.

Show answer

B. Soil nitrogen is a confounder. Adjusting for it, or randomizing fertilizer, recovers the real effect.

3A paper reports 95% accuracy on 40 test samples and no interval. What's your first move?

  • A Wilson interval on 40 samples is wide; differences of a few points can be noise.

  • High accuracy on a tiny test set is weak evidence, and you also need the baseline.

  • A small test set is a limitation to weigh, not proof the result is wrong.

Show answer

A. A Wilson interval on 40 samples is wide; differences of a few points can be noise.

4A model's top feature for predicting hospital readmission is "number of medications". What can you conclude?

  • That's a causal claim. Sicker patients take more medications and are readmitted more; the feature is likely a proxy for illness.

  • Predictive importance describes the model. Causal claims need a design that handles confounders.

  • Possibly, but importance alone doesn't show leakage; it shows reliance.

Show answer

B. Predictive importance describes the model. Causal claims need a design that handles confounders.

Key takeaways

  • A testable question names a population, the model's inputs, a comparison, an outcome metric with its test set, and a threshold fixed before the results.
  • Prediction asks what will happen; explanation asks what would change if you intervened. A good predictor can be a useless lever.
  • A confounder affects both treatment and outcome, and can make a real effect vanish or a fake one appear.
  • Read papers for claim, data, baselines, metrics, and effect size with uncertainty; compute the interval yourself when a paper omits it.
  • Search Scholar, PubMed, and arXiv with exact phrases and field filters, then follow references backward and citations forward.

#Further reading

  • To Explain or to Predict? (opens in a new tab) by Galit Shmueli: the clearest account of why predictive and explanatory modeling need different methods, with examples from several sciences.
  • Leakage and the Reproducibility Crisis in ML-based Science (opens in a new tab): Kapoor and Narayanan's project page, with the civil war case study and the table of fields where ML errors were found.
  • PubMed User Guide (opens in a new tab): field tags, Boolean rules, and filters, with worked search examples.

What you'll learn

  • Store a research question as data and check it for missing parts.
  • Turn reported accuracies and test-set sizes into Wilson confidence intervals and majority-class baselines.
  • Flag weak evidence with explicit rules: no baseline, a baseline inside the interval, random-row splits, too few independent sites.
  • Compute Cohen's d from reported means and standard deviations, and see why a small p-value can hide a trivial effect.
  • Save the table and a falsifiable hypothesis into the project.

A literature review usually ends up as a pile of PDFs and a paragraph that says "previous studies achieved 81 to 97% accuracy." That sentence hides everything that matters: which of those numbers came from 60 test images, which ones beat a real baseline, and which ones were tested on farms the model had never seen.

We're going to build the alternative, a table that recomputes what each paper's own numbers support. Here's where we'll end up:

The six studies are invented for this exercise, but each one has a problem that turns up constantly in real literature. The question they're all about is the one from the last lesson: detecting nitrogen deficiency in wheat from leaf images.

#Step 1: Write the question down as data

A question that lives in a dictionary can be checked by code and saved with the project. This function lists any of the five parts (plus the test set) that are missing or blank.

The threshold is concrete enough to fail. If the model beats the meter by 3 points, the answer is no, and the plan says so before anyone has seen a result.

#Step 2: Enter what each study reports

Read each paper for the five referee questions and record only what it actually states. NaN means "not reported", which is itself information.

Two columns deserve a comment. farms counts independent sources, not images: 2,000 photos from two farms are closer to two samples than 2,000 when the question is about new farms. positive_rate is the fraction of deficient plots in the test set, which papers usually report somewhere in the data section even when they don't report a baseline.

#Step 3: Add the numbers the papers left out

Two numbers can be recomputed from what's already in the table. The Wilson interval comes from accuracy and test-set size. The majority-class accuracy, what you'd score by always guessing the more common class, comes from the positive rate.

Study C's 90% looks respectable until you see that only 12% of its test plots were deficient, so guessing "healthy" every time scores 88%. Its model adds 2 points over a guess that needs no images at all. Study E's 97% sits on 80 images, and its interval stretches from about 91% to over 99%.

#Step 4: Flag the weak spots automatically

Writing the rules as code forces you to state them precisely, and it applies them the same way to the sixth paper as to the first.

Only B and F come through clean, and their accuracies (84% and 88%) are well below the eye-catching 93% and 97% of A and E. That pattern is common: careful evaluation on new farms produces smaller numbers than random splits of images from a few farms, because images from the same farm share soil, lighting, and camera, and a model can learn those instead of the plant.

#Step 5: Plot all the evidence on one scale

A forest plot puts every study's estimate and interval on the same axis, with the two reference points (majority class and the study's own baseline) marked beside it.

Read it row by row: the question for each study is whether the blue interval clears both the grey tick and the orange diamond. For D it doesn't, so "beats logistic regression" isn't supported by D's own test set.

#Step 6: Effect sizes for the field trials

Some papers in a review aren't ML papers at all. Field trials of the fertilizer schedule report mean yields with standard deviations, and the useful summary is an effect size, not a p-value. Cohen's d divides the difference in means by the pooled standard deviation, so it says how many "typical plot-to-plot differences" the treatment moves yield. By Cohen's rough convention, 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium, and 0.8 large.

This is the most misread pattern in research. H passes the usual p < 0.05 test and has a trivial effect: with 2,000 plots per group, a 0.07 t/ha difference is detectable but agronomically meaningless. G has a large effect and p = 0.10, because 12 plots per group can't pin it down. A p-value mixes effect size with sample size; report the effect size and its interval, and the reader can judge both.

#Step 7: Save the table and the hypothesis

The finished review goes into the project, and the plan gains an explicit hypothesis written from what the evidence supports.

#The finished program

Here's the whole review as one standalone cell you can paste into a fresh notebook and point at your own table.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the table record farms separately from n_test?

  • A test set of 80 images from 2 farms is weak evidence about farm number 3, whatever the image count says.

  • The interval uses n_test and accuracy; farms feeds the independence flag.

  • They often don't, which is why a missing value is worth recording.

Show answer

A. A test set of 80 images from 2 farms is weak evidence about farm number 3, whatever the image count says.

2Study C reports 90% accuracy with 12% deficient plots in its test set. What does the table conclude?

  • The headline hides the base rate.

  • The majority-class accuracy is the floor any model must clear, and C barely clears it.

  • Nothing is wrong with the numbers; they just don't support a strong claim.

Show answer

B. The majority-class accuracy is the floor any model must clear, and C barely clears it.

3Trial H has p = 0.046 and d = 0.06. How should it go in your review?

  • A small p-value with 2,000 plots per group mostly reflects the sample size.

  • Report the effect size; d = 0.06 means the groups overlap almost completely.

  • Small effects can be real; they're just small. Exclusion rules belong in the plan, not after the fact.

Show answer

B. Report the effect size; d = 0.06 means the groups overlap almost completely.

Key takeaways

  • Store the research question as data with population, inputs, comparison, outcome, test set, and threshold, and check it with code.
  • Recompute what papers omit: Wilson intervals from accuracy and test size, and the majority-class accuracy from the positive rate.
  • Encode your evidence standards as explicit flag rules so every study is judged the same way.
  • Count independent units (farms, sites, patients), not rows, when judging whether a result generalizes.
  • Report Cohen's d with the p-value; a tiny p from a huge sample can hide a trivial effect.

#Extend it

  • Add a recall column and a second interval for it, since a deficiency detector that misses sick plots is worse than its accuracy suggests.
  • Add a flag for studies whose test set comes from a different season or region than your plan's population.
  • Replace the invented rows with five real papers from your own field, and keep the PDFs' page numbers in a source column.

#Further reading

  • Using Effect Size, or Why the P Value Is Not Enough (opens in a new tab): a short, readable explanation of effect sizes and Cohen's conventions, written for medical researchers.
  • proportion_confint (opens in a new tab): every interval method statsmodels offers for a proportion, including Wilson and the exact Clopper-Pearson interval.
  • ttest_ind_from_stats (opens in a new tab): run a t-test from reported means and standard deviations when you don't have the raw data.

What you'll learn

  • Rewrite vague research ideas into questions with all five parts and a threshold.
  • Classify research goals as prediction or explanation.
  • Expose an accuracy claim that's no better than the base rate.
  • Compare results from test sets of different sizes with confidence intervals.
  • Turn reported means into an effect size and a sentence fit for a report.
  • Write precise searches for Google Scholar, PubMed, and arXiv.

#Warm-up

Run this cell; you'll use missing_parts in Exercise 1. Then, without running anything, say which parts this question is missing: "Does our CNN classify bird calls better?"

(It has the inputs, sort of. "Better" than what, for which birds and recordings, on which test set, and by how much are all missing.)

#Exercise 1: Make three questions testable

Rewrite each idea as a plan dictionary with all six keys filled, so missing_parts returns an empty list.

  1. "Can ML find exoplanets in telescope data?"
  2. "Does machine learning predict air quality?"
  3. "Can AI help diagnose skin cancer?"
Need a hint?

For the comparison, ask what a scientist in that field uses today: a standard pipeline, a simple physical model, or a specialist's judgment. For the test set, name what must be new to the model: new stars, new cities, new clinics.

Show solution

One good answer for the first idea; the other two follow the same pattern.

Air quality: "For PM2.5 monitors in three cities, does a gradient-boosted model predict next-day PM2.5 with lower mean absolute error than persistence (tomorrow equals today), on a later year than training?" Skin cancer: "For dermoscopic images from clinics not used in training, does the model's sensitivity for melanoma at 80% specificity exceed that of general practitioners in a reader study?" Each has a population, inputs, a comparison someone actually uses, a metric, a test set that is genuinely new, and a bar to clear.

#Exercise 2: Prediction or explanation?

Label each goal P (prediction) or E (explanation), and name one variable that could confound the E goals.

  1. Flag which incoming patients are likely to need intensive care in the next 48 hours.
  2. Find out whether a new tutoring program raises exam scores.
  3. Forecast tomorrow's river level from upstream gauges.
  4. Decide whether planting cover crops increases soil carbon.
  5. Sort galaxy images into spiral and elliptical.
Need a hint?

Ask whether the goal involves changing something (a program, a farming practice) and wanting to know the consequence. If it does, it's explanation, and a model with high accuracy doesn't settle it.

Show solution

1 P, 2 E, 3 P, 4 E, 5 P. For goal 2, motivation is a confounder: motivated students are more likely to join the program and to score well anyway. For goal 4, farm management style is one: farmers who plant cover crops often also reduce tillage, which affects soil carbon too. Both are reasons to randomize, or at least measure and adjust for those variables.

#Exercise 3: The 97% that isn't

A paper reports that its model detects a rare heart rhythm in ECGs with 97% accuracy, tested on 1,000 recordings. Its supplementary table gives the confusion matrix: 12 true positives, 18 false negatives, 12 false positives, 958 true negatives. Compute the accuracy, the prevalence, the majority-class accuracy, sensitivity (recall for the rare rhythm), and balanced accuracy.

Need a hint?

Balanced accuracy is the average of sensitivity and specificity, where specificity is TN / (TN + FP). It scores 0.5 for any model that always predicts one class.

Show solution

The model ties a program that always says "normal", and it misses 60% of the rhythms it exists to find. The honest headline is "detects 40% of cases at a 1.2% false-alarm rate," and the paper should have reported sensitivity and specificity, not accuracy.

#Exercise 4: Is the smaller study really better?

Paper P reports 88% accuracy on 60 images. Paper Q reports 85% on 2,000. Compute both Wilson intervals and decide whether P beats Q. Then find the smallest test set for which an 88% accuracy would have an interval no wider than ±2 points.

Need a hint?

For the second part, loop n upward from 100 in steps of 10, compute the interval for round(0.88 * n) correct, and stop when (high - low) / 2 is at most 0.02.

Show solution

P's interval contains all of Q's, so the data can't say P is better. To report 88% to within ±2 points, P would have needed roughly 1,000 test images, about 17 times what it used. Seen that way, a 60-image test set supports "somewhere between the high 70s and low 90s" and nothing finer.

#Exercise 5: Report an effect, not just a p-value

An education study reports final exam scores of 78.4 (SD 10.2, n = 150) for students who used an AI tutor and 76.9 (SD 10.8, n = 150) for those who didn't, and calls the tutor "effective". Compute Cohen's d, the Welch t-test p-value, and a 95% confidence interval for the difference in means. Then write one sentence a careful reviewer would accept.

Need a hint?

The standard error of the difference is sqrt(sd1**2/n1 + sd2**2/n2). For a 95% interval with a sample this large, multiplying by 1.97 (the t critical value for about 300 degrees of freedom) is accurate enough, or use stats.t.ppf(0.975, df).

Show solution

A sentence a reviewer would accept: "Students using the tutor scored 1.5 points higher on average (95% CI −0.9 to 3.9; d = 0.14), a small difference consistent with no effect." It's also not randomized as described, so even a clear difference wouldn't show the tutor caused it.

#Exercise 6: Search like you mean it

You want papers on using machine learning with infrared spectroscopy to identify microplastics in water samples. Write one query each for Google Scholar, PubMed, and arXiv, and describe the next step once you've found one strong paper.

Need a hint?

Scholar uses quotes for exact phrases. PubMed needs uppercase AND/OR and accepts field tags like [tiab]. arXiv is sparse for this topic, so keep that query short.

Show solution

Then snowball: read the strong paper's references for the older work it builds on, and open its Cited by list on Google Scholar for newer work, including any papers that failed to replicate it. Two rounds usually find the core of a niche.

#Challenge: How lucky can a small test set be?

A model's true accuracy on new images is 85%. Each of 20 labs tests a copy of it on its own 50-image test set, and only labs scoring at least 90% bother to publish. Compute the probability that one lab scores 90% or more, check it with a simulation of 10,000 labs, and estimate what the published literature would report as the "typical" accuracy.

Need a hint?

stats.binom.sf(44, 50, 0.85) is the probability of 45 or more correct out of 50. For the simulation, draw rng.binomial(50, 0.85, size=10_000) / 50, keep the scores of at least 0.9, and average them.

Show solution

About one lab in five gets lucky, so a field of 20 labs produces four or five papers, every one reporting 90% or better (about 92% on average) for a model that's really at 85%. Nobody cheated. Small test sets plus selective publication are enough to inflate a literature, which is why you check test-set sizes, look for replications, and treat the most impressive number in a field with the most suspicion.

What you'll learn

  • Ask the provenance questions that reveal how a dataset was collected, labeled, and assembled.
  • Tell missing completely at random, missing at random, and missing not at random apart, and show how dropping rows can bias a result.
  • Detect a batch effect with PCA and a "can a model predict the batch?" test.
  • Explain why randomization, blocking, and controls matter more than any correction applied afterwards.
  • Use statsmodels to find how many samples an experiment needs.

In 2018, a team at Mount Sinai trained a neural network to detect pneumonia in chest X-rays from two hospital systems, and it scored an AUC of 0.93 on held-out images. Then they asked a stranger question: could the network tell which hospital an X-ray came from? It could, for 99.95% of the National Institutes of Health images and 99.98% of Mount Sinai's. That mattered because pneumonia made up 34.2% of the Mount Sinai images and 1.2% of the NIH ones. Simply ranking images by hospital, with no medicine at all, scored an AUC of 0.861. On X-rays from a third hospital system the model's AUC fell to 0.815. (Zech et al., 2018 (opens in a new tab).)

Nothing in the code was wrong. The data carried a fingerprint of where it came from, the label was tied to that fingerprint, and the model used it. Auditing data means finding those fingerprints before your model does.

#Provenance: questions to ask before you train anything

Provenance is the history of a dataset: who collected it, how, and what happened to it since. Ask these before downloading, and record the answers in a file next to the data:

  • Collection. Which instruments, sites, dates, and protocols? Were any changed partway through?
  • Selection. Who or what was included, and who was left out? Volunteers, a single clinic, only the samples that passed quality control?
  • Labels. Who assigned them, using what criteria, and blind to what? Labels from a later test, an expert panel, or text-mined reports differ in quality.
  • Assembly. Is this one study, or several datasets merged? Do the same subjects appear more than once?
  • Processing and license. What was filtered, normalized, or resized before you got it, and are you allowed to use it this way?

The last bullet of "assembly" sank a whole literature. A systematic review of COVID-19 imaging models screened 2,212 studies, kept 62 for detailed review, and judged none of them of potential clinical use (Roberts et al., 2021 (opens in a new tab)). One recurring problem was "Frankenstein datasets", public collections stitched together from other collections, sometimes containing the same images twice. Another was using a pediatric pneumonia dataset as the "not COVID" group, so a model could score well by recognizing children.

#Missing values have a pattern, and the pattern is information

Statisticians sort missingness into three kinds. MCAR (missing completely at random): a vial got dropped, unrelated to anything. MAR (missing at random): missingness depends on something you did record, like a logger that fails in cold weather when you logged the temperature elsewhere. MNAR (missing not at random): missingness depends on the missing value itself, like a sensor that maxes out and records nothing when readings are highest.

This simulated water-quality dataset has the second and third kinds. The turbidity sensor saturates above 16 NTU and reports nothing, and the lake station's thermometer fails in cold water.

Two things stand out. Temperature is missing only at the lake, which a per-site table shows in one line and an overall percentage hides. And samples with missing turbidity bloomed 70% of the time, against 38% for the rest. Dropping incomplete rows, the default in many tutorials, throws away the samples most likely to bloom, and the bloom rate in what's left falls from 0.435 to 0.395. A model trained on complete rows learns from a world with fewer blooms than the real one. Always tabulate missingness by site, by batch, and by outcome before deciding what to do with it.

#Batch effects: when the instrument leaves a fingerprint

A batch is any group of samples processed together: one plate, one sequencing run, one day, one technician. Batches differ in small systematic ways, and with dozens of measured features those small differences add up to a pattern a model can find. Here are 90 samples of 20 gene-expression measurements processed in three runs, with no biological difference between runs at all.

PCA finds the directions along which samples vary most, and the biggest one here is the processing run. A second test makes the same point numerically: if a classifier can predict the batch from the features far better than chance, the batch is in your data.

A batch effect on its own adds noise. It becomes a disaster when the batch lines up with the thing you're studying, as the hospital did with pneumonia in the X-ray study.

#A confounded design can't be rescued afterwards

Suppose you process all 12 treated samples on Monday and all 12 controls on Tuesday. Monday's run reads 1.5 units high. The true treatment effect is 1.0.

The confounded design reports an effect of about 2.3, which is the treatment and Monday's offset welded together. No statistical method can pull them apart, because every treated sample is also a Monday sample, so there's no data on treated Tuesday samples at all. The balanced design, with treatment split evenly within each day, recovers an effect near 1.0 and lets you adjust for day.

That's the case for three habits from experimental design. Randomize which samples get which treatment, using code with a seed, not judgment. Block by batch: balance treatments within each plate, day, or site, so batch can be estimated and removed. Include controls: negative controls (no treatment), positive controls (a known effect, to show the assay can detect one), and if possible the same reference sample on every plate, which measures each batch's offset directly.

#How many samples do you need?

Before running an experiment, ask how many samples it takes to detect the effect you care about. A power analysis answers it from three inputs: the effect size (Cohen's d), the false-positive rate you'll accept (alpha, usually 0.05), and the chance of detecting a real effect that you want (power, usually 0.8).

solve_power solves for whichever argument you leave out. Halving the effect size roughly quadruples the samples needed. And a typical student-sized experiment, 20 per group, has about a one-in-three chance of detecting a medium effect, so a "no significant difference" from it means very little. The effect size you plug in should come from a pilot study or the literature, never from wishful thinking.

⚠️ Watch out

Two audit mistakes that look like rigor. First, "correcting" batch effects in a confounded design: tools like ComBat estimate each batch's offset, and when batch equals treatment they remove the treatment effect along with it. Second, counting rows instead of independent units. Five photos of each of 20 plants is 20 plants, not 100 samples; treating them as 100 makes intervals too narrow and lets the same plant appear in both training and test sets.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A model trained on X-rays from two hospitals scores well internally but poorly at a third hospital. The model can also identify the hospital an image came from. What's the most likely explanation?

  • That's the pattern Zech et al. found: hospital alone gave an AUC of 0.861 because prevalence was 34.2% at one site and 1.2% at the other.

  • Possible in general, but it doesn't explain why the model can identify hospitals so well.

  • Undertraining lowers internal scores too; here internal scores were high.

Show answer

A. That's the pattern Zech et al. found: hospital alone gave an AUC of 0.861 because prevalence was 34.2% at one site and 1.2% at the other.

2A soil moisture probe stops recording when the soil is waterlogged. What kind of missingness is that, and what does dropping those rows do?

  • The missingness depends on the moisture itself, so it isn't random.

  • When the missing value causes the missingness, complete-case analysis distorts the picture.

  • Site doesn't explain it. The missing value itself does.

Show answer

B. When the missing value causes the missingness, complete-case analysis distorts the picture.

3All treated cell cultures were imaged on microscope A and all controls on microscope B. What can analysis do about it?

  • Microscope and treatment are identical columns, so the model can't estimate both.

  • Correction would remove the treatment effect too, since they're indistinguishable.

  • Confounding by design is fixed by design: randomize and block.

Show answer

C. Confounding by design is fixed by design: randomize and block.

4Your pilot suggests d = 0.4. Roughly how does the required sample size compare with d = 0.8?

  • Smaller effects need many more samples.

  • Sample size scales with one over d squared, not one over d.

  • Halving d roughly quadruples n: about 100 per group instead of 26.

Show answer

C. Halving d roughly quadruples n: about 100 per group instead of 26.

Key takeaways

  • Record provenance (collection, selection, labels, assembly, processing, license) before training on any dataset.
  • Tabulate missingness by site, batch, and outcome; MNAR data dropped as "incomplete" biases what's left.
  • Check for batch effects with PCA and by trying to predict the batch from the features.
  • A design where batch lines up with treatment can't be fixed by analysis. Randomize, block by batch, and include controls.
  • Run a power analysis before collecting data; small experiments often can't detect the effects they're looking for.

  • Datasheets for Datasets (opens in a new tab): Gebru and colleagues' template of provenance questions, now widely used to document ML datasets.

A plant pathology lab hands you a pilot dataset. Three greenhouses each measured seedlings with their own handheld spectrometer: reflectance in four bands, three leaves per plant, plus a hand-held chlorophyll (SPAD) reading. Each plant was later scored for powdery mildew. The lab wants a detector that works in any greenhouse, and asks whether this data is good enough to build one.

By the end of this lesson you'll have an audit report and a plan for better data:

#Step 1: Load the pilot and record its provenance

The simulation below stands in for the lab's file. Each greenhouse has a different infection rate and its spectrometer reads each band slightly high or low, the two flaws a real multi-site dataset tends to have.

Now write down what you know about where this data came from, and mark what you don't. The unknowns become your questions for the lab.

"Natural, not inoculated" is the entry to keep an eye on. It means the greenhouses chose their own infection rates, which is how prevalence ended up tied to site.

#Step 2: Count the independent units

The file has 540 rows, but the experimental unit is the plant: three leaves from one plant share its genetics, its pot, and its infection status.

Prevalence ranges from 47% at G1 to 10% at G2. Any feature that identifies the greenhouse now carries information about infection, whether or not it has anything to do with the plant.

#Step 3: Map the missing values

The spectra are complete. SPAD is missing for 42% of G2 readings and nowhere else, so it's missing at random given site. If you used SPAD as a feature, "SPAD is missing" would itself become a G2 detector, and G2 is the low-infection site. The audit decision: leave SPAD out of the detector, keep it for a separate check of the labels, and log the reason.

#Step 4: Look for a site fingerprint

Plot one band by site and infection status before running any model.

Within every greenhouse, infected plants read lower. Across greenhouses, G2's spectrometer reads high and G3's reads low by about as much. Two numbers make that concrete: how well the spectra identify the greenhouse, and how well the greenhouse alone predicts infection.

The spectra identify the greenhouse 94% of the time, and the greenhouse alone predicts infection with an AUC of about 0.72. A model has every incentive to learn the instrument.

#Step 5: Does the score survive a new greenhouse?

The lab wants a detector for any greenhouse, so the honest test holds out a whole greenhouse. Compare that with the usual random split of leaf readings.

The random forest looks excellent on random leaves (0.94) and falls to about 0.80 on a greenhouse it hasn't seen, because it learned the greenhouse-specific readings. The logistic regression holds up much better here: it can only combine bands linearly, and the infection signal is a difference between bands that survives the offsets. That's one pilot, so don't generalize "linear always wins"; the point is that the random split hid a large drop for one model and not the other, and only the grouped split told you which.

#Step 6: Design the follow-up experiment

No analysis can remove the link between site and prevalence in this pilot, because the greenhouses chose their own infection rates. The fix is new data from a design where site can't predict infection:

  • Randomize within each greenhouse, by code with a recorded seed, which seedlings are inoculated with mildew spores.
  • Block by greenhouse: exactly half the plants in every greenhouse are inoculated, so prevalence is 50% everywhere.
  • Controls: mock-inoculated plants (sprayed with water) are the negative control; inoculated plants are a positive control that shows the detector can see real infection. A white reference panel measured at the start of every session records each spectrometer's offset.
  • Blind the person scoring mildew to the treatment.

The crosstab is the proof of balance: 24 and 24 in every greenhouse. The seed means the lab can regenerate this exact layout, and the CSV is what goes to the greenhouse staff.

#Step 7: Size it with a power analysis

Is 48 per greenhouse (72 per arm overall) enough? Take the pilot's within-greenhouse effect on near-infrared reflectance as a starting point, then plan for an effect half that size, because pilot estimates are noisy and inoculated infections may differ from natural ones.

Even planning for half the pilot effect, about 47 plants per arm gives 90% power, and the design has 72. The spare capacity matters for a different reason: the real goal is a detector tested on a held-out greenhouse, which uses only a third of the plants as a test set.

#The finished audit

Here's the audit as one reusable function. Point it at any table with a unit column, a batch column, and a label.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why did the audit count plants instead of using all 540 leaf readings as the sample size?

  • Treating 540 correlated readings as 540 samples overstates the evidence and lets the same plant land in both training and test sets.

  • Speed has nothing to do with it; it's about what counts as an independent observation.

  • The number of leaves is fine. They just add precision to each plant, not new plants.

Show answer

A. Treating 540 correlated readings as 540 samples overstates the evidence and lets the same plant land in both training and test sets.

2The random forest scored 0.94 on random leaves and 0.80 on a held-out greenhouse. Which number goes in the report?

  • It's inflated by greenhouse fingerprints the model will never see in a new greenhouse.

  • The evaluation must match the claim. Report both if you like, but the headline is the held-out greenhouse.

  • Averaging a valid and an invalid estimate doesn't produce a valid one.

Show answer

B. The evaluation must match the claim. Report both if you like, but the headline is the held-out greenhouse.

3Why does the follow-up inoculate exactly half the plants in each greenhouse instead of randomizing across all 144 plants at once?

  • The total is the same; what changes is how treatments are spread across greenhouses.

  • A fully random draw could, by chance, put more inoculated plants in one greenhouse; blocking rules that out.

  • The reason is statistical: balance within each block.

Show answer

B. A fully random draw could, by chance, put more inoculated plants in one greenhouse; blocking rules that out.

Key takeaways

  • Write a provenance record before modeling, and turn its unknowns into questions for whoever collected the data.
  • Count independent units and prevalence per site; a site with a different base rate makes the site itself a predictor.
  • Map missingness by site; a column missing at one site can become a site detector.
  • Test whether features predict the batch, and evaluate on held-out groups that match your claim.
  • Fix confounded data with a new design: randomize within blocks, include positive and negative controls and a reference standard, blind the scorer, and size it with a power analysis that assumes a smaller effect than the pilot.

#Extend it

  • Use the reference-panel idea on the pilot: subtract each greenhouse's mean healthy-plant spectrum and rerun the held-out-greenhouse test. How much of the random forest's drop does it recover, and why is that correction only possible because healthy plants exist in every greenhouse?
  • Add a GroupKFold split by plant to Step 5 and see how much of the random-leaves score came from sibling leaves.
  • Extend audit to report the number of readings per unit and flag units with only one reading.

#Further reading

  • Power and sample size in statsmodels (opens in a new tab): the power classes for t-tests, proportions, and F-tests, all with the same solve_power interface.
  • scikit-learn: cross-validation with groups (opens in a new tab): GroupKFold, LeaveOneGroupOut, and the other splitters that keep related samples together.
  • Datasheets for Datasets (opens in a new tab): a fuller version of the provenance record from Step 1, with questions on motivation, collection, labeling, and maintenance.

m3-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Tabulate missingness by condition and correct an average for data missing at random.
  • Name the missingness mechanism in realistic scenarios.
  • Remove plate-to-plate drift using reference wells.
  • Turn a confounded layout into a randomized, blocked one.
  • Use statsmodels to find sample sizes, power, and minimum detectable effects for means and accuracies.

#Warm-up

A review found that some COVID-19 imaging models used a children's pneumonia dataset as the "not COVID" group. Which provenance question from the Notes lesson would have caught it, and what one-line check on the data would confirm it?

(Selection: who is in each group? Checking the age distribution of each label, for example df.groupby("label")["age"].describe(), would show one group is all children.)

#Exercise 1: When the sensor gives up

A wrist heart-rate sensor loses contact during hard exercise. Run the setup cell, then compute the fraction of missing heart-rate readings for each activity, the mean of the observed readings, and a corrected mean that weights each activity's observed mean by how often that activity occurs.

Need a hint?

wearable.groupby("activity")["heart_rate"].mean() skips missing values within each activity. The weights come from wearable["activity"].value_counts(normalize=True), which counts every row, including those with missing heart rate.

Show solution

The plain average is too low because 40% of the running readings, the highest heart rates, are missing. Since missingness here depends only on activity, which is fully recorded, the data is missing at random given activity, and reweighting by activity recovers the true mean. If the sensor failed because of the heart rate itself (say, above 170 bpm regardless of activity), the data would be MNAR and no reweighting by recorded columns would fully fix it.

#Exercise 2: Name the mechanism

Label each MCAR, MAR, or MNAR, in one sentence each.

  1. A lab tech knocked over a random tray of 8 sample tubes.
  2. People with higher incomes are more likely to skip the income question on a survey.
  3. Older participants are more likely to miss the online follow-up, and age was recorded at enrollment.
  4. A weather station's rain gauge overflows and records nothing during the heaviest storms.
Need a hint?

Ask what the missingness depends on: nothing, a variable you have, or the missing value itself.

Show solution

1 MCAR: which tubes fell has nothing to do with their contents. 2 MNAR: the missing value (income) drives whether it's missing. 3 MAR: missingness depends on age, which you have, so you can adjust for it. 4 MNAR: the gauge fails exactly when rainfall is extreme, so complete cases understate heavy rain.

#Exercise 3: Remove plate drift with reference wells

A plate reader measured 12 sample wells and 3 wells of the same reference standard on each of four plates. The reader drifts between plates. Estimate each plate's offset from its reference wells, subtract it from every well on that plate, and compare sample means per plate before and after.

Need a hint?

The reference standard should read the same on every plate, so each plate's mean reference reading minus the average over all plates is its offset. Use plates["plate"].map(...) to give every row its plate's offset.

Show solution

Before correction, sample means range over about 225 units; afterwards, about 45, which is the sampling noise of 12 wells. The correction works because the reference is the same material on every plate, so any difference in its readings is the instrument. That's why a reference standard belongs on every plate in your design, not just the first.

#Exercise 4: Fix a confounded layout

A student plans to test a grow light: the 10 plants on the window shelf get the grow light, and the 10 on the back shelf don't. Explain the problem, then write code that randomly assigns 5 treated and 5 control plants on each shelf, with a seed, and prints a crosstab proving the balance.

Need a hint?

Loop over the two shelves, and on each one shuffle a list of five "grow light" and five "control" labels with rng.permutation.

Show solution

Shelf and treatment are the same variable: the window shelf also gets more daylight and warmth, so any difference could come from the shelf. Blocking by shelf fixes it.

Now the shelf effect can be estimated (with C(shelf) in a regression) and separated from the light's effect. Moving the grow light between spots also needs some care: light from a treated plant shouldn't spill onto its control neighbors, so leave gaps or use dividers.

#Exercise 5: Three power questions

Use TTestIndPower to answer: (a) how many per group to detect d = 0.3 with 80% power; (b) the power of an experiment with 15 per group if d = 0.6; (c) the smallest effect that 30 per group can detect with 80% power.

Need a hint?

solve_power solves for whichever of effect_size, nobs1, alpha, or power you leave out (or pass as None).

Show solution

Answer (c) is the most useful one to report when you can't change your sample size: "with 30 per group, this study could reliably detect only large effects (d of 0.74 or more)." It tells readers how to interpret a null result.

#Exercise 6: How big a test set to compare two accuracies?

You'll compare a new model with an old one, each on its own independent test set of equal size. How many images does each test set need to detect 90% versus 80% accuracy with 80% power? Use proportion_effectsize and NormalIndPower.

Need a hint?

proportion_effectsize(0.9, 0.8) converts the two proportions into Cohen's h, which plays the role of d for proportions.

Show solution

About 200 images per test set, for a 10-point gap. Smaller gaps get expensive quickly: try 0.85 versus 0.80. Evaluating both models on the same test set and using a paired test needs fewer images, because each image's difficulty cancels out.

#Challenge: Rebuild a Frankenstein dataset

Recreate the pediatric-controls problem. Simulate chest X-ray features where COVID cases are all adults, and controls are children (Frankenstein) or adults (matched). Features: chest_width and bone_density (both depend on age, not disease) and opacity (the real, modest disease signal). Train logistic regression on Frankenstein data, then report its AUC on a Frankenstein test set and on an age-matched test set, and compare with a model that uses only opacity.

Need a hint?

Write one function xrays(n, adult_controls, seed) that draws covid at 50%, sets adult = covid | adult_controls, and makes the age-dependent features from adult. Use roc_auc_score(y, model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]).

Show solution

On the Frankenstein test set the full model is nearly perfect because it's detecting adults. On age-matched patients it collapses toward chance, below the opacity-only model, because the features it leaned on carry no information about disease once everyone is an adult. The opacity-only model's AUC changes only a little, since its signal was real all along. The fix is in the data, not the model: controls drawn from the same population, age, and hospitals as the cases.
