m4-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Build dummy baselines with DummyClassifier and DummyRegressor, and explain what each one measures.
  • Climb a baseline ladder: input-free guess, one-feature rule, linear model, complex model.
  • Judge a gap between models against the spread of scores across seeds.
  • List what a rerun needs beyond a seed: code version, pinned environment, data version, full configuration.

In 2018, a paper in Nature trained a deep neural network to predict where aftershocks would occur after large earthquakes. With 13,451 parameters, it reached an AUC of 0.85, far above the 0.58 of Coulomb stress change, the standard physics-based predictor. A year later, Arnaud Mignan and Marco Broccardo showed that a logistic regression with two free parameters reached the same 0.85, and a logistic regression on distance and mainshock slip reached 0.86 (Mignan & Broccardo, 2019 (opens in a new tab)).

The original paper did compare against a baseline, the one physicists use. What it skipped was the simplest statistical model on the same inputs. That missing rung would have shown that the network's complexity bought nothing, and that the interesting result was in the inputs, not the architecture.

#The baseline ladder

Each rung of the ladder answers a different question, and a result only means something relative to the rung below it.

Rung 1 tells you what score is free. Rung 2 tells you how much one obvious variable explains, the number a domain expert would compute on a napkin. Rung 3 tells you how far a simple combination of features gets you. Rung 4 is only interesting by its margin over rung 3, and only if that margin survives a change of seed.

#Rung 1: models that ignore the inputs

A dummy model predicts without looking at the features. scikit-learn has two: DummyClassifier (strategies include "most_frequent", which always predicts the majority class, and "stratified", which guesses at random in proportion to the class rates) and DummyRegressor (default "mean"). They score what you'd get for free, and they're the quickest check that a metric is behaving.

This dataset has 8% positives, like many screening problems.

The model that never predicts a positive scores 92% accuracy, and logistic regression beats it by only 2 points. On balanced accuracy and AUC, the dummies sit at 0.5 and the real model's advantage becomes visible. That's the dummy's second job: if your chosen metric gives a do-nothing model a high score, choose a different metric before comparing anything else.

#Rungs 2 to 4 on a real dataset

The diabetes dataset in scikit-learn has 442 patients, 10 baseline measurements, and a measure of disease progression one year later. Here are all four rungs, scored with the same 5-fold split. For rung 2, the one-feature rule uses body mass index, the measurement a clinician would reach for first.

The dummy scores about zero, which is what R² is designed to do for a model that predicts the mean. BMI alone gets a third of the way to perfect. Ridge regression on all ten measurements reaches about 0.49, and neither the forest nor the neural network beats it. With 442 patients and a mostly additive relationship, the extra flexibility mostly fits noise. That's not a law (on large datasets with strong interactions, complex models do win), but you only find out which situation you're in by running rung 3.

#One run is one draw: compare gaps with the seed spread

Each score above came from one shuffle of the data into folds and one random initialization of each model. Change the seed and every number moves. Before claiming one model beats another, measure how far scores move when nothing but the seed changes. This cell adds seeds 1 to 4 to the seed-0 scores above.

Ridge barely moves, because its only randomness is the fold split. The neural network moves the most, because each seed also changes its starting weights and its early-stopping validation set. The gap between the forest and the network is smaller than the network's own spread, so "the forest beats the network" isn't supported, while "ridge beats both" holds on every seed. Report the mean and the spread over seeds, never the best seed.

⚠️ Watch out

Three ways papers stack the deck against the baseline. Tuning the complex model's hyperparameters for days while running the baseline with defaults. Scoring the two on different splits, or the baseline on a published number from another paper's data. Running the new model with ten seeds and reporting the best one. Each can manufacture a gap that isn't there. Give every rung the same split, the same tuning budget, and the same number of seeds.

#A seed isn't enough: what a rerun needs

Seeds fix randomness inside one environment. A rerun months later, or by someone else, also needs:

  • The code version. A git commit hash, or at minimum a dated copy of the exact notebook.
  • The environment. requirements.txt with == pins, written when the result was produced, like Module 1 set up.
  • The data version. The SHA-256 of each input file, so a silently edited file is caught.
  • The full configuration. Every hyperparameter, including the defaults you didn't touch, since defaults change between library versions. model.get_params() prints them all.
  • Hardware notes. Multithreaded and GPU code can give slightly different results on different machines. Record the machine, and treat differences in the third decimal as expected rather than alarming.

Published checklists turn this into a list to tick before you submit. The ML Reproducibility Checklist (opens in a new tab) used at NeurIPS covers models, data, code, and results, and the REFORMS checklist (opens in a new tab) from Kapoor, Narayanan, and colleagues is written specifically for ML-based science. The next lesson builds both the baseline ladder and a run record that covers every item above.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A classifier for a rare condition (5% positive) reports 95.4% accuracy. What's the first thing to compute?

  • The model beats doing nothing by 0.4 points. Balanced accuracy or recall will show whether it learned anything.

  • Climbing the ladder starts at the bottom rung; you don't yet know the first model is useful.

  • That tells you about fit, not whether the test score beats a trivial guess.

Show answer

A. The model beats doing nothing by 0.4 points. Balanced accuracy or recall will show whether it learned anything.

2On the diabetes data, ridge regression scored about 0.49 and the random forest about 0.44. What does that suggest?

  • They're often excellent. On this small, mostly additive dataset their flexibility fits noise.

  • The ladder's job is to show where added complexity starts helping. Here it doesn't.

  • More trees reduce variance a little but don't change the underlying bias-variance trade-off much.

Show answer

B. The ladder's job is to show where added complexity starts helping. Here it doesn't.

3Over five seeds, model A scores 0.71 ± 0.04 and model B scores 0.73 ± 0.05. What can you claim?

  • The gap is smaller than either model's seed-to-seed spread.

  • A real difference should be larger than what reshuffling the data produces.

  • Lower variance is nice, but it isn't a higher score.

Show answer

B. A real difference should be larger than what reshuffling the data produces.

4A colleague reruns your notebook with your seed and gets slightly different numbers. Which record would tell you most quickly why?

  • The name doesn't change when the contents, data, or libraries do.

  • Same code can still read different data or run on different library versions.

  • A mismatched hash means different data; mismatched versions point to changed defaults or algorithms.

Show answer

C. A mismatched hash means different data; mismatched versions point to changed defaults or algorithms.

Key takeaways

  • A model's score means something only relative to the rung below: dummy, one-feature rule, linear model, complex model, all on the same split.
  • Dummy models show what score is free and expose metrics that reward doing nothing.
  • Fit a linear model before a deep one; complex models have to earn their place by a margin.
  • Compare gaps between models with the spread across seeds, and report mean and spread, not the best seed.
  • A rerun needs the code version, pinned environment, data hashes, full configuration, and hardware notes, not just a seed.

#Further reading

  • One neuron is more informative than a deep neural network for aftershock pattern forecasting (opens in a new tab): Mignan and Broccardo's preprint, a short and readable case study in the missing linear baseline.
  • scikit-learn dummy estimators (opens in a new tab): every strategy for DummyClassifier and DummyRegressor, with advice on when to use each.
  • REFORMS: consensus recommendations for ML-based science (opens in a new tab): a 32-item checklist covering study goals, data, leakage, metrics, and reproducibility.

m4-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Score a dummy model, a one-feature rule, a linear model, and two ensembles on the same held-out-batch split.
  • Separate variation from held-out batches and variation from seeds.
  • Write a run record with the configuration, data hash, library versions, model parameters, and results.
  • Rebuild the experiment from its configuration alone and prove the record matches.
  • Pin the environment and run an automatic reproducibility checklist.

A protein engineering lab measures the melting temperature (Tm) of enzyme variants: the temperature at which half the protein unfolds. Higher Tm means a more heat-stable enzyme. Each assay batch runs 60 variants, and the lab wants a model that predicts Tm for the next batch from five sequence descriptors, so they can skip variants unlikely to be stable.

Here's the finished result, a ladder of models scored on assay batches they never saw, plus a record that lets anyone regenerate every number:

#Step 1: Fix the configuration, then make and fingerprint the data

Everything that could change a result goes in one dictionary, written before any modeling. The data here is simulated from the config's seed so the lesson runs anywhere; in a real project, make_data would read the lab's file from data/raw instead.

The split is part of the config because it's part of the claim. "Leave one assay batch out" means every score answers the lab's real question: how well does the model do on a batch it wasn't trained on?

#Step 2: Climb the first three rungs

One scoring function serves every rung, which guarantees they all see the same folds and the same metric. Mean absolute error (MAE) is in degrees Celsius, a unit the lab can reason about.

Guessing the training mean misses by 3.5 °C on average. Hydrophobicity alone, a predictor a protein chemist would reach for first, cuts that by a third. Ridge on all five descriptors gets to 1.88. Look at the per-batch numbers too: the same model's error moves by most of a degree depending on which batch is held out, because each batch carries its own calibration offset.

#Step 3: Add the complex rung, with seeds

Random forests and gradient boosting use randomness (bootstrap samples, row subsampling), so each gets run with three seeds. Leave-one-batch-out has no shuffling, so the folds stay fixed and only the models' own randomness changes.

Neither ensemble beats ridge. Gradient boosting comes within about 0.06 °C, a gap far smaller than the 0.38 °C spread across batches, so the honest summary is "ridge and boosting are indistinguishable here, and ridge is simpler". The seed spread is tiny next to the batch spread. That's worth knowing: in this problem, which batch you test on matters far more than which seed you use, so more batches would tighten the comparison more than more seeds would.

#Step 4: Draw the ladder

#Step 5: Write the run record

The record holds everything needed to recognize and regenerate these numbers. get_params() captures each model's full configuration, defaults included, and keeping only the plain values makes it JSON-friendly.

The run ID is a hash of the record's contents, so two runs with any difference in config, data, versions, or results get different IDs. A run ID like that also makes a good name for figures produced from the run.

#Step 6: The whole experiment in one call

This is the finished program. run_experiment starts from nothing but the configuration: it regenerates the data, rewrites and fingerprints the file, scores every rung, and builds the record. If it matches the saved record exactly, the experiment is reproducible on this machine.

If the comparison ever prints False, compare the two dictionaries key by key; the first key that differs (data hash, environment, a model parameter, or a score) tells you where to look.

#Step 7: Pin the environment and run the checklist

The last step writes requirements.txt and runs a checklist against the project folder. Each check is a question a reviewer would ask, written as code so it can't be skipped.

🧪 Try it yourself

Break one check on purpose: add enzymes.loc[0, "tm_c"] += 0.01; enzymes.to_csv(data_file, index=False) as the first line of the checklist cell and rerun it. "data file matches its hash" should fail. Then rerun the Step 6 cell, which rewrites the file from the seed, and the checklist passes again.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does every rung use the same fold_maes function?

  • Different splits or metrics for different rungs is one of the commonest ways a baseline gets shortchanged.

  • There's no such rule; it's a design choice for fairness.

  • Speed is the same. The benefit is that the comparison can't drift.

Show answer

A. Different splits or metrics for different rungs is one of the commonest ways a baseline gets shortchanged.

2Gradient boosting scored 1.94 °C and ridge 1.88 °C, with about 0.38 °C spread across batches. What should the report say?

  • A 0.06 °C gap against 0.38 °C of batch-to-batch spread can't support that.

  • It scored slightly worse, and flexibility isn't evidence.

  • When a complex model doesn't clearly beat a linear one, the linear one wins on simplicity and interpretability.

Show answer

C. When a complex model doesn't clearly beat a linear one, the linear one wins on simplicity and interpretability.

3Why is the run ID a hash of the record's contents rather than a counter like run-002?

  • run-002 is shorter. The point is what the ID guarantees.

  • A counter can be reused or reset; a content hash identifies exactly what was run.

  • They can; they just don't tie the name to the contents.

Show answer

B. A counter can be reused or reset; a content hash identifies exactly what was run.

Key takeaways

  • Put everything that can change a result, including the split and seeds, in one config written before modeling.
  • Score every rung with one function on the same held-out groups, and report the spread across groups and across seeds separately.
  • A complex model earns its place only with a gap larger than the spread; otherwise report the simpler model.
  • Save a run record with config, data hash, versions, full model parameters, and results, and name it by a hash of its contents.
  • Prove reproducibility by rebuilding from the config alone, and turn your standards into a checklist that runs as code.

#Extend it

  • Add a sixth rung, a ridge model with one-hot batch indicators, and explain why it can't help on a batch it has never seen.
  • Make run_experiment accept a data_file argument so the same code runs on the lab's real CSV, and store the file's hash in the run ID.
  • Save the figure from Step 4 as results/figures/<run id>-ladder.png, so every chart can be traced to the run that drew it.

#Further reading

  • pip freeze (opens in a new tab) and the requirements file format (opens in a new tab): the official reference for pinning and reinstalling exact versions.
  • scikit-learn: common pitfalls and recommended practices (opens in a new tab): includes a section on controlling randomness with random_state, and when an integer seed and a generator object behave differently.
  • ML Reproducibility Checklist (opens in a new tab): the one-page checklist from Joelle Pineau used at NeurIPS, a good template for extending Step 7.

m4-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Build a classification baseline ladder and read it with balanced accuracy.
  • Judge a small gap between two models using paired seed-by-seed differences.
  • Locate an edited value with hashes and DataFrame.compare.
  • Report environment drift and write pinned requirements.
  • Audit a run record for missing reproducibility information.
  • Find and remove every hidden source of randomness in a function.

#Warm-up

scikit-learn's breast cancer dataset has 357 benign and 212 malignant tumors. Before running anything, work out what DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent") scores on accuracy and on balanced accuracy. Then check:

(357 / 569 is 0.627. Balanced accuracy averages the recall of each class, 1.0 for benign and 0.0 for malignant, so it's 0.5 for any model that always predicts one class.)

#Exercise 1: The classification ladder

On the same 5-fold split, score four rungs with accuracy and balanced accuracy: the dummy, logistic regression on worst radius alone, logistic regression on all 30 features (scaled), and a random forest with 100 trees. Which rung would you report as the model to beat?

Need a hint?

Keep each rung as a (model, columns) pair in a dictionary, like the build-along, and use make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)) for the logistic rungs.

Show solution

One measurement, the radius of the largest cell nuclei, already scores 0.92. The full logistic regression is the model to beat: it's the best rung, and the forest doesn't beat it. A paper proposing a deep network for this dataset would need to clear 0.975 balanced accuracy, not the dummy's 0.5.

#Exercise 2: Is a one-point gain real?

On the wine dataset (178 wines, three cultivars), a colleague says extra-randomized trees beat a random forest. Score both with 30 trees on 5-fold stratified CV for seeds 0 to 9, changing both the split and the model seed each time. Print each model's mean and standard deviation, the mean paired difference, and how many seeds favor extra trees.

Need a hint?

Use the same StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=seed) for both models inside each loop iteration, so their scores are paired by seed. ExtraTreesClassifier lives in sklearn.ensemble.

Show solution

Extra trees come out ahead on most seeds, by under a point on average. That's a consistent but tiny edge: on 178 wines, one more correct prediction is worth 0.56 points, so the whole gap is about one bottle. A fair report says "extra trees were slightly and fairly consistently better (+0.7 points, ahead on 8 of 10 seeds)", which is very different from "extra trees outperform random forests".

#Exercise 3: Which value changed?

Two copies of a field log are supposed to be identical. Compare their SHA-256 hashes, and if they differ, find exactly which cell changed.

Need a hint?

Hash each file's bytes with hashlib.sha256(Path(...).read_bytes()).hexdigest(). For the cell, read both CSVs back and call first.compare(second), which shows only the cells that differ.

Show solution

The hashes tell you that something changed in a fraction of a second, even for gigabyte files. compare tells you what: row 2's yield went from 6.8 to 6.3. Tools like DVC apply the same idea to whole data folders, storing a hash for every file alongside your git history.

#Exercise 4: Report environment drift

A run record from last year says the result came from numpy 1.26.4, pandas 2.1.4, scikit-learn 1.4.2, and scipy 1.11.4. Print which packages differ from the current environment, then print the pinned requirements.txt lines that would rebuild last year's environment.

Need a hint?

importlib.metadata.version(name) gives the installed version. The pinned lines come straight from the recorded dictionary, not from the current environment.

Show solution

If last year's numbers don't reproduce today, this report is the first place to look. A major-version change (NumPy 1 to 2, for example) can change defaults and random streams, so the fix is to rebuild the old environment from the pinned list, reproduce the old number, and only then upgrade and record what changed.

#Exercise 5: Audit a run record

Write audit_record(record) that returns a list of problems: no seed in the config, no data hash, any requirement without ==, a result without a spread, or fewer than two rungs. Test it on the record below, which has five problems.

Need a hint?

Use record.get("config", {}) so a missing key doesn't crash the audit. A result has a spread if its dictionary has any key starting with "sd".

Show solution

The single result fails two checks at once, the spread check and the rungs check. The most serious problem is the last one: a gradient boosting AUC of 0.91 with no baseline can't be judged at all.

#Exercise 6: Hunt down hidden randomness

This function returns a different score every time it's called. Find all three sources of randomness, then write stable_score(data, seed) that returns the same score on every call with the same seed.

Need a hint?

Look for anything that shuffles or samples: a pandas method, a model, and a splitter. Each takes a random_state argument.

Show solution

data.sample, RandomForestClassifier, and the shuffling StratifiedKFold each drew from an unseeded generator. Seeding all three from one seed argument makes the function a pure function of its inputs, and the "other seeds" line keeps you honest about how much the score moves anyway.

#Challenge: Reproduce a number from a vague methods section

A report says: "We fit ridge regression to the scikit-learn diabetes data, holding out 25% of patients as a test set, and obtained a test R² of 0.527." It doesn't give the split's random seed or the ridge penalty. Search random_state from 0 to 19 and alpha in 0.01, 0.1, and 1.0 for combinations within 0.002 of 0.527. Then report the full range of test R² across your search.

Need a hint?

Loop over both, call train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=rs), fit Ridge(alpha=a), and store (rs, a, score) rows in a DataFrame you can filter.

Show solution

Several different settings reproduce the reported number, so you can "reproduce" it without knowing what the authors actually ran. Worse, the same model and data give a test R² anywhere from about 0.35 to 0.60 depending only on which patients land in the test set. One train/test split is a single draw from that range. A methods section needs the seed and every hyperparameter, and a result needs cross-validation or repeated splits to show where in the range it falls.

m5-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain why a test-set accuracy is a sample statistic with its own standard error.
  • Tell apart SD, SE, and 95% confidence-interval error bars, and compute each.
  • Build a bootstrap confidence interval by hand with NumPy, then with scipy.stats.bootstrap.
  • Choose between a confidence interval and a prediction interval, and compute both with statsmodels.

Your new classifier scores 0.87 on a 150-sample test set. The published baseline scored 0.83 on a test set of the same size. Before you write "our method improves accuracy by 4 points," run the cell below. It imagines a single model whose true accuracy on the whole population is exactly 0.85, then scores it on 10,000 different 150-sample test sets. Guess first: how often does that one model land at 0.87 or above?

A quarter of the test sets give 0.87 or more, and another quarter give 0.83 or less, from a model that never changed. A 4-point gap on 150 rows is not yet a finding; it might be the luck of which rows landed in each test set. This module is about measuring that luck.

#Where the wobble comes from: the standard error

Think of the test set as a poll. You can't test every possible patient, cell, or galaxy, so you test 150 and report the share the model got right. A different 150 would give a slightly different share.

Let's make that precise. If each test row is an independent draw and the model is right with probability p, the number correct is binomial, and the standard error (the standard deviation of the observed accuracy across possible test sets) is

SE = √( p(1 − p) / n ).

The cell checks the formula against simulation for several test-set sizes:

The formula matches simulation to the third decimal, so you can get an SE from a single test set by plugging in your observed accuracy for p. Notice it shrinks with √n, not n: going from 150 to 600 rows only halves it. A rough 95% range is the estimate ± 2 SE, so 0.85 on 150 rows means "somewhere around 0.79 to 0.91."

#SD, SE, and a confidence interval are three different error bars

Many papers draw a whisker on a bar and never say what it is. The three common choices answer different questions:

Error bar Formula Answers
SD (standard deviation) spread of the individual measurements How variable are the things I measured?
SE (standard error of the mean) SD / √n How much would my mean move if I repeated the study?
95% CI mean ± t × SE What range of true means is consistent with my data?

Here are seedling root-growth rates (mm per day) measured on 5, 20, and 80 plants from the same simulated population:

The SD doesn't shrink as you measure more plants; it just homes in on the true 1.1 (five plants give a noisy 1.84), because it describes the plants. The SE and CI keep shrinking, because they describe your knowledge of the mean. ddof=1 divides by n − 1, the usual sample SD, and stats.t.ppf(0.975, df=n-1) is the 95% multiplier for a small sample: 2.78 for n = 5, near 1.96 for large n.

⚠️ Watch out

Unlabeled whiskers. The same data drawn with SE bars looks about four times more precise than with SD bars when n = 16. If a figure or table says "0.91 ± 0.02" without naming the quantity, you can't interpret it. Write it out every time: "mean ± SD across 5 folds" or "95% bootstrap CI."

#The bootstrap: let your sample stand in for the population

Those formulas only exist for simple statistics. What's the standard error of a median, an AUC, or the gap between two models? The bootstrap handles all of them with one idea: you can't draw new samples from the population, so draw them from your sample. Pick n rows with replacement (some appear twice, some not at all), recompute the statistic, and repeat thousands of times. The spread of those values estimates the spread across real repeated studies.

Step through three resamples of a five-value sample and watch resample fill up with repeats:

Now a realistic case: hours until 25 seeds germinate. Germination times are skewed (most seeds sprout together, a few lag far behind), so the median is the natural summary and no simple SE formula applies.

The percentile interval is just the middle 95% of the bootstrap values. It's lopsided (about 4 hours below the median, 11 above), which is the right answer for skewed data and something a symmetric ± formula can't give you. The lumpy histogram is normal for a median: it can only take values that are in the data or halfway between two of them.

SciPy packages the same procedure. Note that data is a tuple of samples, even when there's only one:

The default method, BCa (bias-corrected and accelerated), shifts the percentile cut-offs to correct for bias and skew in the bootstrap distribution. Here it agrees with the percentile interval; with skewed means or small samples it often won't, and BCa is usually the better-calibrated one. The rng= keyword is for SciPy 1.15 and newer; older versions call it random_state=.

#Confidence interval for the line, prediction interval for the next point

Regression adds a second question that people constantly mix up. A chemist builds a calibration curve: absorbance of 6 standard concentrations, each prepared three times. Two questions can be asked at 5 mg/L:

  • Where is the average absorbance at 5 mg/L? That's a confidence interval for the fitted line.
  • Where will the next single sample at 5 mg/L read? That's a prediction interval, and it must also include the scatter of individual measurements around the line.

statsmodels computes both from one fitted OLS model:

Now test what each band promises. The cell draws 10,000 new single readings at 5 mg/L from the true process and counts how many land inside each band:

The confidence interval catches only about 40% of new readings because it was never meant to: it's a statement about the mean. The prediction interval catches almost all of them (95% is the average over many repeated calibrations, so one calibration can land a little above or below). If your model will be used on individual cases, the prediction interval is the honest error bar.

⚠️ Watch out

Bootstrapping rows that aren't independent. If 600 rows come from 30 patients, resampling rows pretends you have 600 independent people, and the interval comes out far too narrow. Resample patients, keeping each patient's rows together. You'll build this cluster bootstrap in the practice lesson.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1A paper reports "accuracy 0.91 ± 0.02" and nothing else. What can you conclude?

  • That reading assumes the ± is a 95% CI half-width, and the paper didn't say so.

  • Those three differ by large factors, so the same "± 0.02" can mean very different precision.

  • You'd need to know what the 0.02 measures before you could back out a sample size.

Show answer

B. Those three differ by large factors, so the same "± 0.02" can mean very different precision.

2You grow a test set from 150 rows to 600 rows. What happens to the standard error of accuracy?

  • SE scales with 1/√n, and √4 = 2.

  • Four times the rows divides the SE by √4 = 2.

  • The model is the same, but your estimate of its accuracy gets more precise with more rows.

Show answer

B. Four times the rows divides the SE by √4 = 2.

3A lab will use your calibration curve to read single unknown samples. Which interval should go in the report next to each reading?

  • That covers the average response at that concentration, not one new measurement.

  • A single new reading has the line's uncertainty plus the measurement scatter, and only the prediction interval includes both.

Show answer

B. A single new reading has the line's uncertainty plus the measurement scatter, and only the prediction interval includes both.

Key takeaways

  • A test-set score is a sample statistic with SE ≈ √(p(1−p)/n); 150 rows give roughly ±6 points at 95%.
  • SD describes the measurements, SE describes the mean, a CI gives a plausible range for the truth. Label which one you drew.
  • The bootstrap resamples your data with replacement to get the uncertainty of any statistic; scipy.stats.bootstrap uses BCa by default. Resample the independent unit, not the row.
  • Use a confidence interval for a mean or a fitted line, and a prediction interval for the next individual observation.

#Further reading

  • Krzywinski & Altman, "Error bars" (Nature Methods, 2013) (opens in a new tab): a two-page guide to reading SD, SE, and CI bars, with the rules of thumb for when overlapping bars mean anything.
  • scipy.stats.bootstrap documentation (opens in a new tab): the full API, including paired=True for statistics of two matched samples and how BCa is computed.
  • statsmodels get_prediction (opens in a new tab): the method behind both bands in the calibration chart.

m5-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Score several models on identical repeated cross-validation folds and summarize the spread, not just the mean.
  • Compute a paired difference between two models and explain why the naive interval for it is too narrow.
  • Bootstrap a locked test set for each model's accuracy and for the paired difference.
  • Draw a comparison figure with labeled intervals and write a result sentence a reviewer can check.

A state environmental agency samples 480 lakes once each summer and wants an early warning for harmful algal blooms. Your colleague trained a random forest and says it "beats logistic regression." By the end of this build you'll have the figure and sentence that either support that claim or say how far the data can actually go. Here's the plan:

The data are simulated, so we know the truth: blooms switch on when water passes about 23 °C and the lake stratifies, and phosphorus matters more in warm lakes. A random forest can learn that threshold; a linear logistic model can only approximate it. The forest should be somewhat better. The question is whether 480 lakes are enough to show it.

#Step 1: Simulate the lake survey

Each row is one lake, sampled once, so rows are independent. (Module 6 deals with data where they aren't.)

A third of lakes bloom, so a model that always says "no bloom" already scores about 0.66. That's the number every other model has to beat, and it belongs in the final figure.

#Step 2: Lock away a test set before anything else

All model choices happen on the 360 development lakes. The 120 test lakes are scored once, at the end, so they give an estimate nobody tuned toward.

#Step 3: Score every model on the same 25 folds

RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, n_repeats=5) runs 5-fold cross-validation five times, reshuffling between repeats, which gives 25 scores per model. Because cv is one object with a fixed random_state, every model sees exactly the same 25 train/validation splits. That pairing is what makes Step 4 possible.

The log transform tames the right-skewed chemistry columns and is harmless for the rest, since every column is positive. Now read the table across, not down. Logistic regression's folds range from 0.71 to 0.92: one lucky fold would have made it look better than the forest's average. The forest's mean is 2.7 points higher, but its worst fold and logistic regression's best fold overlap heavily. You can't decide from means.

#Step 4: Compare on paired folds, and correct the interval

Since both models were scored on the same folds, subtract fold by fold. Pairing cancels the "this fold was easy" effect that hits both models together.

The naive interval treats the 25 differences as 25 independent experiments and excludes zero. They aren't independent: any two folds share most of their training lakes, and across repeats the same lakes are validated again and again. The differences rise and fall together, so 25 of them carry far less information than 25 separate studies would.

Nadeau and Bengio's correction inflates the variance to account for that overlap: replace 1/k with 1/k + n_val/n_train. With 5-fold CV, n_val/n_train = 0.25, which here is more than six times larger than 1/k = 0.04, so the interval widens about 2.7×. Now it runs from −1.0 to +6.4 points. The forest winning 18 of 25 folds sounds decisive, but it's the same overlap problem in a friendlier costume.

📝 Note

The correction is a heuristic, not an exact result. In Nadeau and Bengio's simulations it kept false alarms near the promised 5%, while the naive t-test declared differences that weren't there far more often.

#Step 5: Bootstrap the locked test set

Fit each model once on all 360 development lakes and record, for every test lake, whether it was classified correctly. A vector of 1s and 0s is all the bootstrap needs.

Look at the third-to-last line. The models agree on 102 of the 120 lakes, so the whole comparison rests on 18 lakes. That's why the paired difference has a wide interval even though each accuracy looks precise to within a few points. row_diff is +1 where only the forest was right, −1 where only logistic regression was, and 0 elsewhere; bootstrapping its mean resamples lakes, keeping each lake's two predictions together. That's a paired bootstrap, and it's narrower than comparing two separate intervals would be.

#Step 6: Draw the comparison figure

The left panel shows what each model achieves; the right panel shows the quantity the claim is actually about, the difference, with a reference line at zero.

The intervals in the legend and axis labels say exactly what they are. The x-axis on the left isn't forced to start at zero: this is a dot plot, and dots are read by position, so a zoomed axis is fine. (Bars are read by length, which is why truncated bar charts mislead; Module 7 returns to this.)

#Step 7: Write the sentence that goes in the paper

Both analyses point the same direction, and both intervals include zero. The defensible claim: "Both models beat the majority baseline by 13 to 16 points; the forest may be a few points better than logistic regression, but 480 lakes can't distinguish a gain of 6 points from a small loss." That's a real result. It tells the agency the comparison is worth repeating with more lakes, and it stops anyone from building policy on a 2.7-point gap.

#The finished script

Here is the whole build as one file you can run top to bottom in a fresh Colab runtime:

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the build pass the same cv object to cross_val_score for every model?

  • Paired differences cancel the "easy fold" or "hard fold" effect that hits both models at once.

  • It can (cv=5), but then the folds for each model wouldn't be guaranteed to match.

  • Sharing the splitter doesn't change the number of fits.

Show answer

A. Paired differences cancel the "easy fold" or "hard fold" effect that hits both models at once.

2The forest won 18 of 25 folds. Why isn't that strong support on its own?

  • Win counts don't have a 95% threshold; the issue is what the 25 folds are.

  • That's the same reason the naive interval is too narrow: correlated results get counted as if they were separate experiments.

  • Ties are normal with small validation folds and don't invalidate anything.

Show answer

B. That's the same reason the naive interval is too narrow: correlated results get counted as if they were separate experiments.

3On the test set the models disagree on only 18 of 120 lakes. What does that imply for the difference in accuracy?

  • Pairing makes it narrower than naively combining two intervals, but it's still driven by only the disagreements.

  • The 102 lakes where both models agree add nothing to the difference.

Show answer

B. The 102 lakes where both models agree add nothing to the difference.

Key takeaways

  • Score every model on one shared, repeated CV splitter and report the spread of fold scores alongside the mean.
  • Compare models with paired differences. Correct their interval for fold overlap (1/k + n_val/n_train); the naive version is too narrow.
  • Bootstrap the locked test set from a per-row correct/wrong vector, and bootstrap the paired difference, not two separate accuracies.
  • Put the difference, with its interval and a zero line, in the figure. That's the quantity the claim is about.
  • "We can't tell yet, and here's the range" is a reportable result.

#Extend it

  • Change make_lakes(480, ...) to 2,000 lakes. Does the corrected interval for the gap move off zero? Roughly how many lakes would the agency need?
  • Swap accuracy for scoring="roc_auc" in Step 3 and sklearn.metrics.roc_auc_score with paired=True bootstrapping of (y_test, scores) in Step 5.
  • Turn the comparison into a one-sided question ("is the forest better?") and compute a corrected p-value with stats.t.sf.

#Further reading

  • scikit-learn: Statistical comparison of models using grid search (opens in a new tab): implements the corrected t-test step by step and adds a Bayesian alternative for "how likely is model A better?"
  • Nadeau & Bengio, "Inference for the Generalization Error" (Machine Learning, 2003) (opens in a new tab): the paper behind the 1/k + n_val/n_train correction.
  • Bouthillier et al., "Accounting for Variance in Machine Learning Benchmarks" (2021) (opens in a new tab): measures how much data splits, seeds, and hyperparameter choices move benchmark results, and what that means for claiming one method beats another.

m5-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Turn a reported mean ± SD into a standard error, a confidence interval, and a test of the difference.
  • Choose the right resampling unit: independent groups, matched pairs, or whole clusters.
  • Bootstrap a test-set AUC and build a split-conformal prediction interval around any regressor.
  • Measure the real coverage of an interval by simulation.

Each exercise gives you a task and the numbers you should land near. Try it in your own notebook first; the solutions build on each other, so run them in order if you open them.

#Warm-up: an accuracy in your head

A plankton-image classifier gets 0.92 accuracy on 60 test images. Without code, estimate its standard error and a rough 95% range. Then work out how many test images you'd need for the 95% range to be ±0.02.

Need a hint?

SE = √(p(1 − p)/n). For the second part, set 1.96 × SE = 0.02 and solve for n.

Show solution

About ±7 points on 60 images. Getting to ±2 takes more than ten times as many images, because the SE shrinks with √n. (Near 0.99 the normal approximation gets poor; Exercise 5's bootstrap or a Wilson interval handles that.)

#Exercise 1: Decode a reported error bar

A paper's table says enzyme activity was 12.4 ± 2.1 in treated cultures and 10.1 ± 1.9 in controls, n = 8 cultures each, with "±" defined as SD in the methods. Compute each group's SE and 95% t-interval. Do the intervals overlap? Then run Welch's t-test from the summary numbers alone.

You should find intervals of about 10.6 to 14.2 and 8.5 to 11.7, and a p-value below 0.05.

Need a hint?

scipy.stats.ttest_ind_from_stats(mean1, std1, nobs1, mean2, std2, nobs2, equal_var=False) needs no raw data.

Show solution

The intervals overlap by about a unit, yet the difference is significant at the 5% level. Overlapping 95% CIs do not mean "no difference": the uncertainty of a difference is √(SE₁² + SE₂²), which is smaller than SE₁ + SE₂. Compare groups with an interval or test on the difference itself.

#Exercise 2: Bootstrap a difference in medians between two groups

Days to first flower for 24 shaded and 24 sunny plants (generated below). Bootstrap a 95% CI for median(shaded) − median(sunny). The two groups are independent plants, so each group should be resampled separately.

You should get a gap of 8.3 days with an interval that stays above zero but is wide.

Need a hint?

Pass both samples in the tuple: bootstrap((shaded, sunny), statistic, ...). SciPy resamples each one independently unless you set paired=True. Give your statistic an axis argument so SciPy can vectorize it.

Show solution

The interval excludes zero, so shade plausibly delays flowering, but "somewhere between 1.5 and 12.5 days" is the honest size of the effect. Report the range, not just "significant."

#Exercise 3: Bootstrap a correlation, keeping the pairs together

Thirty finches each have a beak-depth and a seed-hardness measurement. Bootstrap the Pearson correlation two ways: correctly (resample birds, so each bird's two numbers stay together) and incorrectly (resample each column on its own). Explain the difference.

Need a hint?

paired=True tells bootstrap to draw the same row indices from every sample. For the wrong way, call rng.choice on each column separately.

Show solution

Resampling the columns separately scrambles which beak goes with which seed, so every resample has a true correlation of zero. The "interval" is centered on 0 and describes no birds that exist. Resample the unit you measured: here, the bird.

#Exercise 4: Twelve mice, six measurements each

Blood glucose was measured 6 times on each of 12 mice. Mice differ from each other (SD 1.0) much more than one mouse varies day to day (SD 0.5). Compute a 95% interval for the overall mean by (a) resampling the 72 rows and (b) resampling mice with all their measurements. Which is right, and by roughly what factor were the naive intervals too narrow?

Need a hint?

For (b), draw 12 mouse indices with replacement, concatenate those mice's arrays, and take the mean. A mouse picked twice contributes all 6 of its values twice.

Show solution

Resampling mice gives an interval a bit over twice as wide. The study has 12 independent animals, not 72, and a mouse's six readings mostly repeat the same information about that mouse. The cluster bootstrap respects that. A quick cross-check: a t-interval on the 12 per-mouse means gives a similar width.

#Exercise 5: An interval for a test-set AUC

Train a logistic regression on simulated biomarker data for 300 patients and score 120 new ones. Report the test AUC with a 95% bootstrap interval.

Expect an interval roughly ±0.1 wide around 0.67.

Need a hint?

The AUC needs each patient's label and score together, so use paired=True. roc_auc_score can't take an axis argument, so add vectorized=False. Use method="percentile" and 1,000 resamples to keep it fast.

Show solution

An AUC of 0.67 on 120 patients is compatible with anything from "barely better than a coin" to "moderately useful." A test set that small can't pin down a modest AUC, which is worth saying in the abstract, not just the supplement.

#Exercise 6: A prediction interval for any model

The statsmodels prediction interval only works for linear regression. Split conformal prediction works for any regressor: fit on one part of the data, measure absolute errors on a separate calibration part, and use a high quantile of those errors as the ± for new predictions. Build a 90% interval for a ridge model on load_diabetes and check its coverage on a test part.

Use a 50/25/25 split. You should see coverage near 90%.

Need a hint?

With n calibration errors, use the ⌈(n + 1)(1 − α)⌉ / n quantile, with method="higher". The +1 is what makes the guarantee hold for finite n.

Show solution

The guarantee is about averages over many calibration sets, so one run can land a few points above or below 90%. The interval has the same width for every patient; extensions such as conformalized quantile regression let it widen where the model is less sure.

#Challenge: Does a 95% interval cover 95% of the time?

"95%" is a promise about repeated studies. Test it. Draw 1,000 datasets of size n from an exponential distribution with true mean 1. For each, build a 95% percentile-bootstrap interval for the mean (1,000 resamples) and a 95% t-interval, and count how often each contains 1. Do it for n = 10 and n = 50.

Need a hint?

Vectorize the resampling: d[rng.integers(0, n, (1000, n))].mean(axis=1) gives 1,000 bootstrap means in one line.

Show solution

At n = 10 with skewed data, neither interval keeps its promise, and the percentile bootstrap is the worse of the two (around 84%). The bootstrap's sample is a stand-in for the population, and ten values from a skewed distribution are a poor stand-in. At n = 50 both get close to 95%. This is why BCa exists, and why "I bootstrapped it" doesn't make a tiny sample trustworthy.

m6-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain group, temporal, and spatial leakage, and pick the scikit-learn splitter that prevents each one.
  • Run an ablation study that removes one component at a time and read the result for shortcuts.
  • Check whether a conclusion survives different random seeds and hyperparameters.
  • Recognize the forking-paths problem and name three ways to defend against it.

A team records a phone's accelerometer while 30 people hold it still, 16 recordings per person. Half the people have a movement disorder. The team trains a 5-nearest-neighbor classifier and checks it with 5-fold cross-validation. Then a reviewer asks for one change: keep all of each person's recordings in the same fold. Same model, same data, same metric. Guess how much the score moves.

From 0.88 to 0.61. Only the question changed. KFold asked "can you label a new recording of someone you've already met?" GroupKFold asked "can you label a new person?" Only the second matches how the model would be used.

#Group leakage: the model learned who, not what

Each person has a movement signature that shows up in every one of their recordings, and it's larger than the condition's effect on any single feature. With shuffled folds, a test recording's nearest neighbors are almost always other recordings of the same person, whose label is right there in the training set. The classifier is doing person identification and getting diagnosis for free.

That's leakage: information unavailable at prediction time gets into training and inflates the score. Whenever rows come in groups (patients, mice, plots, lab batches, sessions), split on the group.

This failure is not hypothetical. Zech and colleagues (PLOS Medicine, 2018) trained pneumonia detectors on chest X-rays from several hospital systems and found the networks could identify which hospital system an X-ray came from for more than 99.9% of images. Because pneumonia was 34% of one hospital's images and about 1% of another's, sorting by hospital alone gave an AUC of 0.86. A model can score well by learning the source of the data.

#Time and space leak the same way

A river sensor logs daily water temperature and dissolved oxygen for two years. Oxygen depends on temperature, plus a slow drift that carries over from day to day. A tempting feature is simply the day number. Compare shuffled 5-fold CV with forward-chaining splits that always train on the past and test on the next three months:

Shuffled CV says adding the day number cuts the error in half. Forward-chaining says it does nothing. With shuffled folds, every test day sits between training days from the day before and the day after, so the forest just reads off its neighbors' drift. When you actually forecast, tomorrow has no neighbors in the training set. test_size=91 keeps every training window at least a year long so each fold sees a full season.

Space works the same way. Soil samples a few meters apart are more alike than samples a kilometer apart, so random folds let a model interpolate between neighbors and overstate how well it maps new ground. Cut the map into blocks and use the block as the group; you'll build this in the practice lesson.

#Ablations: take components away one at a time

An ablation study removes one part of a system (a feature block, a preprocessing step, a model component), re-runs the same evaluation, and records how much the score drops. It answers "what is this result made of?" Use the honest, grouped splitter, and repeat it over several split seeds so each number comes with a spread.

Read it row by row. Removing the tremor block costs about 2 points, removing the device feature costs 6, and the noise floor on its own scores best of all. That feature measures the phone, and the phone tells you the clinic, and the clinic tells you who was recruited where. The ablation didn't find the biology; it found the recruitment pattern. The next check would be leave-one-clinic-out validation, where that shortcut can't help.

Removing gait slightly improves the score and removing grip changes almost nothing, but both are within about one seed-to-seed SD of the full model, so neither is a finding.

#Sensitivity: would another reasonable choice change the conclusion?

A sensitivity analysis reruns the study under choices you could reasonably have made differently: seeds, hyperparameters, preprocessing, thresholds. If the headline flips, the headline was about the choice. Here is the neighbor count k swept under both splitters:

Leakage doesn't just inflate the number; it changes which model you'd pick. KFold favors small k (find the same person), GroupKFold favors large k (average over many people). Seeds are a sensitivity check too: the ablation's "SD over seeds" column, about 0.02 to 0.03, is the noise floor of this evaluation. A claimed improvement smaller than that needs more data before it means anything, and reporting only your best seed is a quiet way of reporting noise.

#Forking paths: try 30 analyses and one will look good

Every choice you make while looking at results (which features, which model, which outlier rule) is a fork. Take enough forks and you'll find a path that looks good by chance. To see how strong the effect is, build a dataset where the labels are pure noise, try 30 random four-feature subsets, and keep the best:

The best analysis reaches 0.65 on labels that contain no information, and falls back to chance on new data. Cross-validation was done correctly every time; the leak is in the selection. A famous demonstration is the fMRI study that found "significant" brain activity in a dead salmon (opens in a new tab), because thousands of voxels were tested without correction. Three defenses work: decide the comparisons before you look (and write them down), correct for the number of tests (Holm or Benjamini–Hochberg), and confirm the final choice on a test set that played no part in the search.

⚠️ Watch out

Preprocessing on the full dataset. Scaling, imputing, selecting features, or oversampling before splitting lets test rows shape the training pipeline. Put every data-dependent step inside a Pipeline so cross_val_score refits it on each training fold. Feature selection is the worst offender: on pure noise it can push a CV score from 50% to over 90%.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A dataset has 400 skin-lesion photos from 80 patients, 5 photos each. Shuffled KFold gives 0.93; GroupKFold by patient gives 0.78. Which number belongs in the paper?

  • Its test photos have siblings from the same patient in training, which won't be true for new patients.

  • The splitter has to mirror deployment; here that means whole patients held out.

  • Averaging an inflated estimate with an honest one is still inflated.

Show answer

B. The splitter has to mirror deployment; here that means whole patients held out.

2In the ablation, the noise-floor feature alone beat the full model. What's the best next step?

  • That feature encodes which clinic recorded someone, which won't predict the condition anywhere else.

  • If the score collapses when clinics are held out, the feature is a shortcut, not a symptom.

  • Model capacity isn't the problem; what the feature measures is.

Show answer

B. If the score collapses when clinics are held out, the feature is a shortcut, not a symptom.

3You tried 30 feature sets and report the best CV score, 0.65. Which change fixes the optimism?

  • The problem is choosing the maximum of 30 noisy scores, which more folds don't remove.

  • A held-out test set (or nested CV) gives an estimate that the selection couldn't tune toward.

  • That's less inflated, but it no longer describes the model you're actually claiming.

Show answer

B. A held-out test set (or nested CV) gives an estimate that the selection couldn't tune toward.

4Shuffled KFold says a "day number" feature halves forecasting error; TimeSeriesSplit says it doesn't help. Why the difference?

  • In real forecasting there's no tomorrow in the training set, so the trick disappears.

  • The temperature-only model scores about the same under both splitters; only the day feature changes.

Show answer

A. In real forecasting there's no tomorrow in the training set, so the trick disappears.

Key takeaways

  • Leakage means information unavailable at prediction time reaches training. Split on the unit you'll predict for: groups with GroupKFold, time with TimeSeriesSplit, space with blocks.
  • Leaky CV inflates scores and picks different hyperparameters, so fixing it can change your whole conclusion.
  • An ablation removes one component at a time under the same honest evaluation; a feature that works suspiciously well alone is a shortcut to investigate.
  • Rerun across seeds and reasonable settings. A gain smaller than the seed-to-seed spread isn't a finding.
  • Searching many analyses and reporting the best one is selection leakage; pre-specify, correct, and confirm on untouched data.

#Further reading

  • Kapoor & Narayanan, "Leakage and the Reproducibility Crisis in ML-based Science" (2022) (opens in a new tab): a survey of leakage errors across 17 fields and 329 papers, with an eight-part taxonomy and a reproduction showing complex civil-war prediction models lose their edge once leakage is fixed.
  • scikit-learn: cross-validation iterators for grouped and time-series data (opens in a new tab): pictures of exactly which rows each splitter holds out, including StratifiedGroupKFold and LeaveOneGroupOut.
  • Zech et al., "Variable generalization performance of a deep learning model to detect pneumonia in chest radiographs" (PLOS Medicine, 2018) (opens in a new tab): the hospital-shortcut study, readable without deep-learning background.

What you'll learn

  • Write scikit-learn transformers whose preprocessing is learned from training folds only.
  • Measure how much row-level cross-validation overstates a multi-site result.
  • Produce an ablation table and chart with seed-to-seed error bars.
  • Separate model-seed, split-seed, and hyperparameter sensitivity, and summarize all checks in one audit table.

An agronomy group wants to flag nitrogen-deficient soil from near-infrared (NIR) reflectance so farmers can skip expensive lab tests. They collected 20 soil cores at each of 16 farms. The lab scanned the cores in four batches, four farms per batch, and the scanner was recalibrated between batches. Their draft reports 0.80 accuracy. You're the internal reviewer, and you'll produce three checks and one table:

#Step 1: Simulate the study

Three things in this generator matter later: each farm has its own soil texture that shifts every band, each lab batch has its own instrument offset, and deficiency rates differ by farm (partly because rain leaches nitrogen).

Farm deficiency rates run from 15% to 85%. That spread is what makes farm-level leakage dangerous: if the model can recognize a farm, it can guess that farm's usual answer without reading the spectrum at all.

#Step 2: Make every preprocessing step learn from training rows only

Two preprocessing ideas come from the group's draft. Batch centering subtracts each batch's average spectrum to cancel the scanner offset. A nitrogen index, band 1700 minus band 1200, contrasts the band that drops most with one that barely moves. Batch centering learns something (the batch means), so it must be fit on training rows. Writing both as scikit-learn transformers puts them inside the pipeline, where cross_val_score refits them on every training fold.

The on= switches are there for the ablation: every variant is the same pipeline with one switch flipped, so nothing else changes between rows of the table. Following scikit-learn's conventions (store constructor arguments unchanged, put learned values in attributes ending with _) is what lets cross_val_score clone these steps safely.

#Step 3: Leakage check, rows versus farms

There's the draft's 0.80, and it drops by about 14 points once whole farms are held out. Under KFold, every test core has 15 or so cores from the same farm in training, with the same rainfall, elevation, and soil texture. Rainfall and elevation are constant within a farm, so they work as a farm ID. The agronomists want a model that works on a new farm, so the rest of the audit uses farm-level splits only.

#Step 4: The ablation table

StratifiedGroupKFold keeps farms whole and roughly balances deficiency across folds. Each variant runs with four seeds; every seed changes both the forest and the fold assignment, so the spread covers both sources of noise.

First, the full pipeline scores 0.70 here, not the 0.66 of Step 3's single unshuffled split. One split is one draw, which is why every row uses four. Batch centering is worth about 7 points: without it, the scanner offsets swamp the deficiency signal. The farm covariates are worth about as much, and unlike in Step 3 that's legitimate here, because farm-level CV means the model has to use rainfall on farms it has never seen, and rain truly drives leaching. The nitrogen index adds about a point, which is inside the seed-to-seed spread, so the honest wording is "no measurable benefit," not "the index improves accuracy." The "without spectra" row is a control: spectra contribute about 11 points beyond what farm weather can give.

💡 Tip

Look at the error bar before the bar. A component whose removal changes the score by less than about one SD hasn't been shown to matter, in either direction. Say so explicitly rather than ranking components by tiny means.

#Step 5: Sensitivity to the hyperparameter and to seeds

The forest's min_samples_leaf controls how finely it can carve the data. Sweep it across a 30× range, three seeds each, and separately measure how much the model seed alone and the split seed alone move the score.

The whole 30× sweep moves the mean by about two points, less than the seed noise inside each setting. That's a good outcome: the conclusion doesn't depend on a lucky hyperparameter. The two seed SDs are similar in size, which tells you that rerunning with a different random_state in either place can shift the headline by a couple of points. Both should appear in the methods.

#Step 6: Assemble the audit

That last paragraph can go into a methods section nearly as is. It names the splitter, the unit, the number of seeds, what ± means, and the inflated number that a careless analysis would have reported.

#The finished script

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why is batch centering written as a transformer instead of subtracting batch means from the whole dataset before cross-validation?

  • Means computed on all rows would include the test fold's spectra, a small but real leak.

  • It can; the point is when the means are computed, not whether pandas can do it.

  • A forest accepts any numeric matrix; the transformer exists for leak-proof evaluation.

Show answer

A. Means computed on all rows would include the test fold's spectra, a small but real leak.

2Rainfall and elevation were a leak in Step 3 but a legitimate gain in Step 4. What changed?

  • The pipeline is identical; only the splitter changed.

  • When a farm's cores span train and test, a constant farm value acts as an ID; when the farm is held out entirely, it can only help if rain really relates to deficiency.

Show answer

B. When a farm's cores span train and test, a constant farm value acts as an ID; when the farm is held out entirely, it can only help if rain really relates to deficiency.

3Removing the nitrogen index changes the mean by about −0.01 with a seed-to-seed SD of about 0.015. How should the paper describe the index?

  • A one-point change inside seed noise isn't an improvement you've demonstrated.

  • That states the result and its precision without claiming more than the data show.

  • Negative and null ablation results tell readers what the result does not depend on.

Show answer

B. That states the result and its precision without claiming more than the data show.

Key takeaways

  • Put every step that learns from data (scaling, batch correction, selection) inside the pipeline so each fold refits it.
  • Group-level CV can turn a "leaky" covariate into an honest one: the same feature can be a farm ID or a real predictor depending on the split.
  • An ablation is only as good as its error bars. Changes within the seed-to-seed spread are "no detectable effect."
  • Run the sweep and the seed checks together. A conclusion that survives a 30× hyperparameter range and several seeds is robust; report both kinds of noise.
  • End with a table of checks, results, and decisions, plus a sentence that names the splitter, unit, seeds, and what ± means.

#Extend it

  • Add a "leave one batch out" check with LeaveOneGroupOut on soil.batch. What happens to batch centering when the test batch has no training rows, and what would a real lab need to do (run reference samples in every batch)?
  • Ablate two components at once (centering and covariates). Is the combined drop the sum of the individual drops?
  • Replace the forest with logistic regression and rerun the ablation. Do the same components matter?

#Further reading

  • scikit-learn: Common pitfalls and recommended practices (opens in a new tab): the official page on preprocessing leakage and controlling randomness, with short examples of each.
  • scikit-learn: Developing estimators (opens in a new tab): the conventions BatchCenter follows, and why breaking them makes cloning in cross-validation fail.
  • Lones, "How to avoid machine learning pitfalls: a guide for academic researchers" (2021) (opens in a new tab): a checklist-style tour of design, evaluation, and reporting mistakes, including ablations and multiple comparisons.

m6-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Match a cross-validation splitter to how a dataset was collected.
  • Find and fix leaks from oversampling and from centered rolling windows.
  • Decide whether a claimed improvement is larger than seed-to-seed noise.
  • Apply Bonferroni, Holm, and Benjamini–Hochberg corrections and explain the trade-off.
  • Detect redundant components that one-at-a-time ablation hides, and quantify spatial and tuning optimism.

#Warm-up: pick the splitter

For each study, name the scikit-learn splitter you'd use and what you'd pass as groups, if anything.

  1. 2,000 retinal scans from 500 patients, both eyes, two visits each.
  2. Hourly air-quality readings from one station for three years; the model will forecast the next day.
  3. 10,000 satellite pixels labeled as forest or farmland, from one region.
  4. 800 independent survey responses, 12% positive.
Show solution
  1. GroupKFold or StratifiedGroupKFold with groups=patient_id. Eyes and visits of one patient share almost everything.
  2. TimeSeriesSplit, ideally with a gap (gap=24) between training and test so the last training hours don't sit right next to the first test hour.
  3. GroupKFold with groups set to spatial blocks (grid cells several times larger than the distance over which neighboring pixels look alike).
  4. StratifiedKFold(shuffle=True). The rows really are independent, and stratifying keeps the rare class in every fold.

#Exercise 1: The oversampling leak

A rare-event dataset has 8% positives. A labmate duplicates positive rows until the classes balance, then runs 5-fold CV with a random forest and reports recall 1.00. Reproduce the leak, then oversample correctly: inside each training fold only, scoring on untouched test rows.

Expect the correct recall to be far below 1.

Need a hint?

Loop over cv.split(X, y). Call oversample on the training indices only, fit, and compute recall_score on the original test rows.

Show solution

Oversampling first puts copies of the same positive row in both training and test folds, and a forest recognizes an exact copy perfectly. Done inside the training fold, recall is honest and low, which is the real news: this model barely finds the rare class. (The imbalanced-learn library's Pipeline does the in-fold version automatically.)

#Exercise 2: A rolling mean that sees the future

A lake buoy logs daily chlorophyll, and you want to forecast tomorrow's value. Someone adds a 7-day smoothed feature with rolling(7, center=True). Compare it with a trailing window, rolling(7), and with today's value alone, using TimeSeriesSplit and mean absolute error.

Need a hint?

A centered 7-day window at day t averages days t − 3 through t + 3. Which of those days include the value you're trying to predict?

Show solution

The centered window includes tomorrow (and the two days after), so it "forecasts" better than anything honest. TimeSeriesSplit didn't catch it, because the leak is inside each row, not between folds. The trailing window is no better than today's value alone, which is the true answer for this series. Check every feature's time window, not just the splitter.

#Exercise 3: Is the gain bigger than the seed?

A labmate reports that adding a new feature to a breast-cancer classifier raised CV accuracy from 0.937 to 0.940, using random_state=3. Rerun the comparison with ten split seeds (same folds for both models within a seed) and decide.

Need a hint?

For each seed, build one StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=seed) and pass it to both cross_val_score calls. Then look at the mean and SD of the paired gains.

Show solution

The gain averages essentially zero and is positive in only some seeds. Seed 3 happened to be one of the best. The "new feature" here is random noise, which is the point: a +0.3-point gain is what noise looks like at this sample size. Report the mean and spread over seeds, decided before you look.

#Exercise 4: Fifteen biomarkers, three corrections

You test 15 blood biomarkers between 25 patients and 25 controls with t-tests. In this simulation markers 1 to 3 truly differ and the other 12 don't. Which markers pass at p < 0.05 uncorrected, after Bonferroni, after Holm, and after Benjamini–Hochberg?

Need a hint?

multipletests(pvals, alpha=0.05, method=...) returns a tuple whose first item is a boolean array of rejections. The method names are "bonferroni", "holm", and "fdr_bh".

Show solution

Uncorrected testing finds all three real markers plus one false one. Bonferroni and Holm control the chance of any false positive, so they drop the false marker but also lose a real one. Benjamini–Hochberg controls the expected share of false discoveries, keeping all three real markers here and dropping the false one. Use Holm when a single false claim is costly; use BH for screening, where some false leads among many are acceptable.

#Exercise 5: The ablation that misses redundancy

A field station predicts whether a plot needs irrigation from two soil-moisture probes (two readings each) plus air temperature and wind. Run a one-at-a-time ablation removing probe A, then probe B. Then remove both. What does the single-removal table fail to show?

Need a hint?

Write a helper that takes a list of columns and returns the mean 5-fold CV accuracy of model, then call it on four column lists.

Show solution

Removing either probe alone costs between 0 and 3 points, which might tempt you to write "soil moisture barely matters." Removing both drops accuracy by about 21 points. Each probe covers for the other. When components are correlated, ablate them as a group too, and report which groups you tested.

#Exercise 6: Spatial blocks

Six hundred soil samples are scattered over a 10 km × 10 km area, and their carbon content follows a smooth spatial pattern plus an elevation effect. Compare a 10-nearest-neighbor regressor's R² under random KFold and under GroupKFold on 2.5 km grid blocks.

Need a hint?

A block ID is (x // 2.5) * 4 + (y // 2.5), which numbers the 16 cells of a 4 × 4 grid.

Show solution

Random folds let every test sample borrow from neighbors a few hundred meters away, so the model looks like an excellent map-maker. With whole blocks held out it must predict into unsampled territory, and R² falls by more than half. Which number to report depends on the claim: interpolating within a densely sampled field, or mapping a new one.

#Challenge: How optimistic is tuning without nesting?

On 100 rows of pure noise, tune an RBF SVC over 20 combinations of C and gamma with GridSearchCV and report best_score_. Then estimate performance honestly with nested CV: the grid search runs inside each outer training fold, and the outer test fold scores whatever it picked.

Need a hint?

Nested CV is one line: pass the unfitted GridSearchCV object as the model to cross_val_score with a different outer splitter.

Show solution

best_score_ is the maximum of 20 noisy CV scores, the same forking-paths problem from the notes, so it overstates chance-level data by about 10 points. Nested CV never lets the outer test fold influence the choice, and it lands near 0.5. Use best_score_ to choose settings, never as the result.
