m7-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Distinguish reproducible, replicable, robust, and generalisable results.
  • Pick a published result that is checkable with your data, code, and compute.
  • Decide whether a reproduced number is consistent with a claim using intervals for both.
  • Keep a discrepancy log, use the REFORMS checklist, and write methods, limitations, and figures that a reader can verify.

For years, papers on predicting civil war onset reported that random forests and other complex models far outperformed logistic regression. Then Sayash Kapoor and Arvind Narayanan reran those papers from their published replication materials. Every claim of superiority failed to reproduce. The gains came from data leakage (one paper imputed missing values in the training and test data together; another used proxies for the outcome), and once that was fixed the complex models did no better than logistic regression (their write-up (opens in a new tab)). No new data, no new method, just careful rerunning. That's what a reproduction can do.

Most reproductions are less dramatic: you get a number that's close but not equal and must decide what that means. A documented "we got 88.5%, they reported 91.2%, and here's whether that gap matters" is a contribution. Hiding it, or quietly tuning until the numbers match, is not.

#Four ways to get "the same result"

People use these words loosely, and fields disagree (the ACM once used "reproducible" and "replicable" the opposite way). This course follows The Turing Way, which sorts results by whether the data and the analysis are the same as the original:

  • Reproduction reruns the same analysis on the same data. With the authors' code, it's computational reproduction; from the paper's description alone, it's reimplementation (much more informative, and much harder).
  • Robustness keeps the data but changes reasonable choices: another splitter, another library, another seed.
  • Replication applies the same method to new data, such as a newer survey or another hospital.

A result can reproduce perfectly and still fail to replicate, which usually means the finding was specific to its dataset.

#Choose a result you can actually check

A good target for a student reproduction has five properties:

  1. One specific number in a table or figure, not "our method works well."
  2. Public data, ideally the exact version the paper used, with a stated sample size.
  3. A method described well enough to rebuild: model, features, preprocessing, split, metric.
  4. Compute you have. A logistic regression on 500 rows: yes. Retraining a model that took 64 GPUs: pick one table row that doesn't need that.
  5. A claim that matters. If the number were wrong, someone's conclusion would change.

A partial reproduction of one well-chosen row beats an unfinished attempt at the whole paper. Write down what you're attempting, and what you aren't, before you start.

#Decide what "reproduced" means before you run anything

If you choose the tolerance after seeing your number, you'll choose one that flatters it. Write it down first. A principled rule uses the uncertainty in both numbers: the paper's accuracy came from a finite test set too.

The Wilson interval is a better-behaved CI for a proportion than ± 2 SE, especially near 0 or 1. The Newcombe interval combines two Wilson intervals into one for the difference. In the first case, a 2.7-point shortfall on 400 images is well within what two independent test sets could produce. In the second, 5.5 points on 2,000 images is not; something about the method or data differs, and your job is to find out what.

Two cautions. The function assumes independent test sets; if you used the paper's exact split, the comparison should be paired, which needs their per-example predictions. And "consistent" isn't "confirmed": it only means this test can't tell the numbers apart. Say how wide the interval was.

#Keep a discrepancy log

Every difference between your setup and the paper's goes in a table as you find it, including ones you think don't matter:

# Difference Paper Reproduction Expected effect Tested?
1 Library MATLAB 2015 scikit-learn 1.8 small no
2 Scaling "normalized" (unspecified) z-score inside each fold unknown yes: tried min-max too
3 Data version 13 variables 13 variables, documented in dataset notes none n/a
4 Split seed not reported 10 seeds, reported mean ± SD none on mean yes

The "Tested?" column is the discipline. If you try three scaling variants, report all three and which one you'd defend in advance, not just the closest to the paper. Hunting through variants until one matches is the forking-paths problem from Module 6 wearing a lab coat.

#Report with a checklist, not from memory

The REFORMS checklist (Kapoor and colleagues, Science Advances, 2024) was written by 19 researchers from computer science, data science, mathematics, the social sciences, and biomedical sciences, specifically for ML-based science. It has 32 items in 8 sections: study design, computational reproducibility, data quality, data preprocessing, modeling, data leakage, metrics and uncertainty quantification, and generalizability and limitations. Fill it in while designing the study: items such as "what population is the claim about?" are easier to answer honestly before the data shape your thinking. Attach it as a supplement. Clinical prediction models have their own standard, TRIPOD+AI, and many ML venues require a paper checklist at submission.

Two parts of the write-up deserve special care.

Methods should let a stranger rerun you. Compare:

Limitations should name specific threats and their likely direction, not apologize in general. "Our sample may not be representative" says nothing. "All 16 farms are in one state's corn belt, so accuracy on sandy coastal soils is untested and likely lower" tells a reader where the claim stops.

#Figures that don't mislead

The most common misleading ML figure is a bar chart of three accuracies with the y-axis starting just below the smallest one. Bars are read by length, so a 2-point difference looks like a tripling. A dot plot with intervals shows the same numbers honestly:

The rules: start bar axes at zero, or use dots when they can't; draw and label intervals; put compared conditions on one axis; and with only a few observations per group, plot them all instead of a bar.

⚠️ Watch out

Tuning the reproduction until it matches. If the first faithful attempt gives 88.5% and you then try twelve variants and report the one that hits 91.2%, you haven't reproduced anything; you've found one path among many that lands near the target. Pre-register the main attempt and its tolerance, log every variant, and report the faithful attempt as the primary result.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1You rerun a paper's code on its own dataset and get the same table. Then you apply the same code to next year's data and the effect disappears. How should you describe the original result?

  • Same data and analysis gave the same answer; new data with the same analysis did not.

  • Robustness is about changing the analysis on the same data, which you didn't do.

  • You did reproduce it; the failure came when the data changed.

Show answer

A. Same data and analysis gave the same answer; new data with the same analysis did not.

2A paper reports 0.950 on 2,000 test images. Your faithful reimplementation gets 0.895 on a fresh 2,000-image split, and the Newcombe interval for the gap is −0.072 to −0.039. What do you write?

  • The gap's interval excludes zero by a wide margin.

  • The gap is real for this setup, so the useful contribution is narrowing down why.

  • Searching for a matching variant turns the reproduction into a forking-paths exercise.

Show answer

B. The gap is real for this setup, so the useful contribution is narrowing down why.

3Which methods sentence lets someone else rerun the evaluation?

  • It gives no splitter, number of folds, grouping, seeds, or summary statistic.

  • Every choice that changes the number is stated.

  • "Standard" means different things in every field; it can't be checked.

Show answer

B. Every choice that changes the number is stated.

Key takeaways

  • Reproduction (same data and analysis), robustness (same data, new analysis), and replication (new data) answer different questions; say which one you did.
  • Choose one specific, checkable number with public data and feasible compute; a careful partial reproduction is a real result.
  • Fix the tolerance before running, using intervals for both the paper's number and yours; a Newcombe interval for the gap that excludes zero means there's something to explain.
  • Log every difference and every variant you try; report the pre-specified attempt as primary.
  • Fill in REFORMS while designing the study, write methods someone can rerun, name specific limitations, and draw dots with intervals instead of truncated bars.

#Further reading

  • REFORMS: Consensus-based Recommendations for Machine-learning-based Science (opens in a new tab): the checklist, its guidelines, and a fillable template; the arXiv version (opens in a new tab) is free to read.
  • National Academies, Reproducibility and Replicability in Science (2019) (opens in a new tab): the U.S. report that settled on working definitions and describes what makes computational results checkable.
  • Weissgerber et al., "Beyond Bar and Line Graphs: Time for a New Data Presentation Paradigm" (PLOS Biology, 2015) (opens in a new tab): shows how very different datasets produce identical bar charts, with practical alternatives.

What you'll learn

  • Turn a published sentence into precise, checkable claims and write the match rule before running anything.
  • Audit a dataset's provenance against its documentation.
  • Reproduce several reported results exactly, and report one that doesn't match along with what was tried.
  • Generate a short reproduction report with a results table, intervals, a figure, a discrepancy log, and limitations.

The wine dataset that ships with scikit-learn has a published result attached. Its documentation, copied from the UCI repository, says the data were used by Aeberhard, Coomans and de Vel (1992) to compare classifiers, and reports:

That's a reproduction target with every property from the notes: specific numbers, public data, simple methods, seconds of compute. By the end you'll have this report, generated from your own results:

#Step 1: Write the claims and the match rule first

Leave-one-out (LOO) on 178 wines means each accuracy is a count out of 178, so turn each percentage back into a number of errors. That tells you exactly what you're trying to match.

Only one decimal place was reported, but at n = 178 each wine is worth 0.56 points, so the counts are unambiguous: 7 errors for 1NN, 2 for LDA, 1 for QDA, none for RDA. RDA (regularized discriminant analysis, Friedman 1989) isn't in scikit-learn, so this is a partial reproduction of three of the four numbers. Say that now, not at the end.

#Step 2: Audit provenance

Check the data against its own documentation before modeling. The UCI page says 178 wines from three cultivars, class sizes 59, 71, and 48, 13 chemical measurements.

Everything matches. One line in the UCI notes matters, though. The donor wrote that "the initial data set had around 30 variables," that only the 13-variable version was donated, and that they no longer knew which 13 those were. If the 1992 study used a different set of variables, no amount of modeling care will make every number match. That goes in the discrepancy log as an unresolvable difference.

#Step 3: Reproduce LDA and QDA

cross_val_predict with LeaveOneOut fits 178 models, each on 177 wines, and returns the held-out prediction for every wine. Counting the mismatches gives the LOO errors directly.

Two exact matches, on scikit-learn defaults, three decades and several programming languages later. That's a strong reproduction: LDA and QDA are deterministic, so either you get the same count or something differs.

#Step 4: 1NN on z-transformed data, and a discrepancy

"z-transformed" has two reasonable readings: z-score all 178 wines once (what a 1992 paper most likely did), or z-score inside each LOO fold (what we'd do today to avoid leakage). The primary attempt is the first, the closer reading of the paper; the second is a pre-declared variant.

Eight errors instead of seven: 95.5% against a claimed 96.1%, one wine apart. Both readings of "z-transformed" agree, so scaling leakage isn't the explanation (with LOO, one held-out row barely moves the means and SDs).

Now the temptation. You could try Manhattan distance, other scalers, or ties broken differently until something gives 7. Instead, run a small, declared sensitivity check and report all of it, whichever way it lands:

Manhattan gives 4 errors, unscaled gives 41. So the 1NN result is very sensitive to the distance and scaling choices, and the paper's "z-transformed" with Euclidean distance is the closest match to their number. None of the variants hits 7 exactly, and that's fine: the job was to test, not to match. The honest summary is "not exactly reproduced; off by one wine; consistent within sampling error; likely causes are a different data version or unreported details of the distance or tie-breaking."

#Step 5: Put intervals on everything and draw the comparison

With 178 wines, a Wilson interval tells you how much any of these numbers could move by chance alone.

The intervals are wide (about ±3 points for 1NN), which cuts both ways. Our 1NN result is consistent with the claim, and the claimed ranking of QDA above LDA (one wine apart) is far inside the noise. This dataset can't tell those two methods apart, a point the original one-decimal table doesn't make.

#Step 6: Generate the report

The report is built from the variables, so rerunning the notebook updates it. Nothing is typed by hand.

md_table writes Markdown by hand so the cell needs no extra packages; paste the output into a .md file or a notebook text cell. The report states the claim, the pre-set rule, the outcome in one sentence, the results table, everything that differed, and where the conclusions stop. It also says plainly what wasn't attempted.

#The finished script

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the build convert 96.1% into "7 errors out of 178" before running anything?

  • With LOO on 178 wines, accuracy only comes in steps of 1/178, so the error count is what you're actually matching.

  • It reports accuracy just as easily; the conversion is about defining the target precisely.

  • The conversion makes the comparison stricter, not looser.

Show answer

A. With LOO on 178 wines, accuracy only comes in steps of 1/178, so the error count is what you're actually matching.

21NN gives 8 errors instead of 7. Manhattan distance gives 4. Why not report Manhattan, since it's at least as good?

  • It's a perfectly reasonable distance; the problem is choosing it after seeing results.

  • Variants go in a sensitivity table, all of them, and the pre-declared attempt stays the headline.

  • Distance from the claim is exactly the wrong reason to choose an analysis, in either direction.

Show answer

B. Variants go in a sensitivity table, all of them, and the pre-declared attempt stays the headline.

3The claimed QDA and LDA results differ by one wine, and both reproduced exactly. What does the report say about which method is better?

  • One wine out of 178 is far inside the ±2 to 3 point intervals.

  • Reproducing a number exactly doesn't make the difference between two numbers meaningful.

Show answer

B. Reproducing a number exactly doesn't make the difference between two numbers meaningful.

Key takeaways

  • Convert published percentages back into counts when the sample size allows; that's the precise target.
  • Write the match rule and the primary analysis before running, and declare which claims you won't attempt.
  • Check the data against its documentation; a provenance note (such as "originally ~30 variables") can explain a gap that modeling never will.
  • When one result doesn't match, run a small, declared sensitivity check and report every variant, not the closest.
  • Generate the report from the notebook's variables, with intervals, a discrepancy log, and limitations, including what reproducing exactly does not show.

#Extend it

  • Check robustness: rerun LDA and QDA with RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=10, n_repeats=5) and compare the mean ± SD with the LOO results.
  • Try scikit-learn's QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis(reg_param=...) as a related but different method to RDA, and label it that way in the report. If you choose reg_param with LOO on the same data, the score will be optimistic; nest it.
  • Find another dataset with a reported result in its documentation (the Wisconsin breast-cancer data's notes report 97.5% from repeated 10-fold CV on three features) and run the same workflow.

#Further reading

  • UCI Machine Learning Repository: Wine (opens in a new tab): the dataset page with the original notes, the donor's comment about variables, and links to the papers.
  • Aeberhard, Coomans & de Vel, "Comparative analysis of statistical pattern recognition methods in high dimensional settings" (Pattern Recognition, 1994) (opens in a new tab): the journal version of the comparison behind the numbers.
  • scikit-learn: Linear and Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (opens in a new tab): how both classifiers work and what the shrinkage and reg_param options change.

What you'll learn

  • Name what kind of check a study performed: reproduction, robustness, replication, or generalisation.
  • Decide whether a reproduced number differs from a claim by more than sampling error.
  • Catch percentages that can't arise from the stated sample size.
  • Write checkable methods, redraw a misleading chart, and audit a paper against REFORMS.
  • Diagnose a failed reproduction by comparing two pipelines.

#Warm-up: what kind of check is it?

Label each with reproduction, robustness check, replication, or generalisation (in the Turing Way sense).

  1. You rerun a paper's notebook on its released data and get the same table.
  2. You use the paper's data but switch from 5-fold CV to leave-one-site-out and from R to Python.
  3. You apply the paper's exact pipeline to a dataset collected two years later at a different hospital.
  4. A different team, with different data and a different method, reaches the same conclusion.
Show solution
  1. Reproduction: same data, same analysis.
  2. Robustness check: same data, different (reasonable) analysis choices.
  3. Replication: different data, same analysis.
  4. Generalisation: different data and different analysis, same answer. This is the strongest of the four and the rarest.

#Exercise 1: Is the gap bigger than chance, at two sizes?

A paper reports 87.0% accuracy on 230 held-out patients. Your reimplementation scores 83.5% on a fresh 230-patient split from the same source. Is the gap consistent with sampling error? Then answer again assuming both test sets had 2,300 patients and the same accuracies.

At n = 230 the gap's interval should cross zero; at n = 2,300 it shouldn't.

Need a hint?

Convert each accuracy to a count of correct patients, then use proportion_confint(..., method="wilson") for each and confint_proportions_2indep(mine, n, theirs, n, method="newcomb") for the gap.

Show solution

The same 3.5-point gap is "consistent" with 230 patients and "a real difference" with 2,300. Small test sets make almost any reproduction look successful, which is why the report should give the interval's width, not just the verdict.

#Exercise 2: Percentages that can't exist

A test-set accuracy computed on n cases must equal k/n for some whole number k. A paper reports these results. Which are impossible at one decimal place?

Reported Test cases
93.8% 97
94.0% 97
71.4% 35
88.2% 51
65.0% 43

This is the idea behind the GRIM test (opens in a new tab) (Brown and Heathers, 2016), which found impossible means in a large share of the psychology papers it could check.

Need a hint?

For each row, loop over k = 0 … n, round 100k/n to one decimal, and see whether any match the reported value.

Show solution

94.0% of 97 falls between 91/97 (93.8%) and 92/97 (94.8%), and 65.0% of 43 falls between 28/43 (65.1%) and 27/43 (62.8%). An impossible value isn't proof of anything bad (it may be a typo, a different n after exclusions, or a different metric), but it's a concrete question to ask the authors and a line in your discrepancy log.

#Exercise 3: Rewrite a vague methods paragraph

Rewrite this so a stranger could rerun it. Use the lake-bloom study from Module 5's build as the facts.

Need a hint?

Name: the data (how many lakes, how sampled, outcome definition), every preprocessing step and where it was fit, the models and their settings, the splitter, repeats and seeds, the metric and what ± means, the test set, and the comparison's interval.

Show solution

"82% accuracy" became a number with a design, an interval, and a comparison. "Performed best" became a difference whose interval includes zero, which is the actual finding.

#Exercise 4: Redraw a misleading figure

This figure reports a new pipeline's 5-fold CV results. Redraw it so a reader can judge the comparison.

Need a hint?

Plot every fold as a point (a fold appears in all three columns, so you can connect them with faint lines), add the mean ± SD, and label what the bars mean. Use an axis range that shows the fold spread.

Show solution

The redraw shows what the bars hid: fold-to-fold spread (about 0.03) is larger than the gap between pipelines, but within each fold pipeline B is slightly ahead. That paired pattern is the real argument for B, and it calls for the paired, corrected interval from Module 5, not a taller bar.

#Exercise 5: Audit a paper with REFORMS

Read this description and list the problems, grouped by REFORMS section (study design; computational reproducibility; data quality; data preprocessing; modeling; data leakage; metrics and uncertainty; generalizability and limitations).

Need a hint?

Ask, for each step: was it fit on training data only, and would the model have this information at prediction time? Then ask what the numbers are being compared to.

Show solution
REFORMS section Problem Fix
Study design The claim's population and use are undefined, and "outperforming prior work" compares numbers from different datasets. State who the model is for; rerun the prior method on the same data.
Computational reproducibility "Code available on request," no versions or seeds. Public repository, pinned environment, seeds.
Data quality No inclusion criteria; "readmission" undefined (this hospital only?). Describe the cohort, the label, and its source.
Data preprocessing Unclear whether imputation and feature selection used all data. Fit both inside the training pipeline.
Modeling Hyperparameters tuned on the test set. Tune with CV on training data; touch the test set once.
Data leakage Random split of admissions puts the same patients in both sets; a random split across 2015–2022 lets the model train on the future. Group by patient; train on earlier years, test on later ones.
Metrics and uncertainty One AUC from one split, no interval, no calibration. Bootstrap CI, calibration plot, repeated or temporal validation.
Generalizability and limitations One hospital, no external validation, no limitations stated. Test at another site, or state that it's untested.

Tuning on the test set and splitting admissions instead of patients could each inflate the AUC by a lot. The 0.91 is uninterpretable until both are fixed.

#Exercise 6: Is a reproduced ranking robust?

In the build, QDA (1 LOO error) and LDA (2 errors) both reproduced exactly on the wine data. Check whether "QDA beats LDA" survives a robustness check: 10-fold stratified CV repeated 10 times, paired fold differences, and the corrected interval from Module 5.

You should find a difference under one point with an interval that includes zero.

Need a hint?

Use one RepeatedStratifiedKFold object for both models. For 10-fold CV, n_val/n_train = 1/9.

Show solution

Most folds are ties, because both classifiers are nearly perfect on this data. The ranking from 1992 reproduces numerically, but it doesn't show that QDA is the better method here. A reproduction report can say both things.

#Challenge: Diff two pipelines to find the leak

A paper says: "Missing values were imputed with feature means, and a standardized logistic regression was evaluated with stratified 5-fold CV. Accuracy: 0.84." Their released code is paper_pipeline below. Your reimplementation from the text is my_pipeline. Run both, find the line that explains the gap, and check whether the plain reading of "imputed with feature means" (one mean per column computed on all data, outside CV) is also leaky, and by how much.

Need a hint?

Look at what paper_pipeline groups by before computing the fill value. What would it need to know about a new patient to impute that patient's missing values the same way?

Show solution

The paper's code fills each missing value with the mean of that row's class. A missing value therefore becomes a coded hint about the label, and with 40% of values missing there are many hints. At prediction time you don't know the class, so this can't be done, and the 0.84 is mostly leakage. Filling with overall means outside CV is a much smaller problem here, within a point or two of the in-fold version, but it's still the wrong order and costs nothing to fix. The report should say: "not reproduced; the released code imputes using class labels; corrected accuracy 0.65," which mirrors what happened in the civil-war reproductions.

What you'll learn

  • Pick a reproduction target that fits your skills, data access, and compute.
  • Check whether the target number can be distinguished from nearby values at its sample size.
  • Write a pre-registration plan: claim, match rule, primary analysis, declared variants, controls, and exclusions.
  • Lay out milestones so the study is finished, tested, and written up on time.

Your capstone is a reproduction study of one published machine-learning result. Not a whole paper: one claim, one table row or figure, reproduced carefully enough that a reader trusts your verdict whether it matches or not. A clean "we reproduced 2 of 3 numbers exactly, the third is off by one sample, and here is everything we tried" is a complete, publishable-quality capstone. So is "the headline doesn't reproduce, and here's the leak."

#What you'll hand in

  1. A notebook that runs top to bottom in a fresh Colab runtime and regenerates every number and figure in the report.
  2. A report of about 4 to 6 pages: research context, the claim, data provenance, methods, baseline and controls, results with uncertainty, ablation or sensitivity analysis, error analysis, discrepancy log, limitations, and a reproducibility statement.
  3. The REFORMS checklist, filled in for your study, with "not applicable" where it truly isn't.
  4. A 5-minute talk (slides or a poster) aimed at someone who hasn't read the paper.

Every one of those must survive the question "how do you know?" The rest of this module is about making sure they do.

#Five project ideas

Each comes with a real source, a specific target, and the twist that makes it interesting. Data for the first three ship with scikit-learn or are pure simulation; the last two need a download inside your own Colab notebook.

Level Project Target claim Twist
Starter Wine classifiers, finished. Aeberhard et al. (opens in a new tab), as in Module 7 RDA 100% by leave-one-out Implement regularized discriminant analysis (Friedman, 1989) yourself, tune it with nested LOO, and see whether 100% survives honest tuning.
Guided The wrong way to cross-validate. Elements of Statistical Learning (opens in a new tab), Section 7.10.2 Selecting 100 of 5,000 noise predictors on all 50 samples, then 1-NN with CV: about 3% average CV error, true error 50% Pure simulation in seconds. The next lesson builds it with you; your job is the extensions.
Medium Breast cancer from three nuclear features. Street, Wolberg & Mangasarian (1993) (opens in a new tab), per the dataset notes One separating plane on worst area, worst smoothness, mean texture: 97.5% by repeated 10-fold CV The three features were chosen by exhaustive search on the full dataset. Does 97.5% hold when the search runs inside each fold?
Harder Fashion-MNIST benchmark. Xiao, Rasul & Vollgraf (2017) (opens in a new tab), Table 3 e.g. RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, criterion="entropy", max_depth=100): 0.873 test accuracy, mean of 5 runs 70,000 images. Plan compute, report seed variance, and compare your spread with "averaged over 5 runs."
Advanced Civil war prediction. Kapoor & Narayanan's reproduction (opens in a new tab) of published political-science models Complex models beat logistic regression; after fixing leakage, they don't Messy real data and someone else's code. Reproduce both the original and the corrected result.

You may propose your own target instead. It must meet the five tests from Module 7: one specific number, public data, a method described well enough to rebuild, compute you have, and a claim that matters.

#Can your target even be tested?

Before you commit, check the resolution of the claim: how far apart two results can be and still be indistinguishable at that sample size. A claim with a ±2-point interval can't confirm or refute a 1-point discrepancy, and your plan should say so up front.

The Fashion-MNIST test set is 56 times larger than the wine data, yet its interval is only about three times narrower, because accuracies near 100% vary less than accuracies near 87%. For CV-based claims such as the breast-cancer one, treating each row's held-out prediction as one test case gives a rough lower bound on the uncertainty. For a simulation claim like ESL's, the resolution comes from the spread across simulations: with 50 runs and a run-to-run SD of about 2 points, the average is pinned down to about ±0.6 points.

#Write the plan before you touch the data

Copy this template into the first text cell of your notebook and fill in every line. Once you've run the primary analysis, don't edit the plan; add dated notes below it instead.

Item 6 is where reproductions usually go wrong. Every paper leaves something unstated: the distance metric, whether scaling happened inside the folds, what "highest correlation" means for negative correlations. Decide how your primary analysis reads each one now, and list the alternatives as declared variants.

Item 9 deserves a control as well as a baseline. A shuffled-label control reruns your whole pipeline with y randomly permuted; it should score at chance. If it doesn't, something is leaking, and you've found it before a reviewer did.

#Milestones

Give M3 the most time. It's where the surprises are, and anything unexpected there changes M4 and M5. If you're short on time, cut the number of variants in M5, never the uncertainty in M4.

⚠️ Watch out

Changing the target after seeing results. If your first run misses the paper's number, it's tempting to switch to a different table row that happens to match. That turns your study into a search for agreement. Keep the target, report the miss, and investigate it; add the second row as an extra, clearly labeled.

💡 Tip

Email isn't off limits. If the paper leaves out a detail you can't resolve, it's normal to write to the corresponding author with one specific question. Log the question, the date, and the answer (or the silence) in your discrepancy table.

Key takeaways

  • One claim, reproduced carefully, beats a whole paper reproduced loosely; matching and not matching are both valid outcomes.
  • Check the target's resolution first: the sample size decides which discrepancies you can detect.
  • Fill in the plan, including the ambiguities, declared variants, and match rule, before the primary run, and don't edit it afterward.
  • Add a shuffled-label control as well as a baseline; it catches leaks early.

m8-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Turn a reproduction plan into code: claim, rule, and declared variants as variables the notebook checks itself against.
  • Build negative and positive controls that show the pipeline can detect both "nothing" and "something."
  • Use a secondary claim in the source to judge between readings of an ambiguous method.
  • Add tests that make the notebook fail loudly if a result drifts, then generate the report from the results.

The Elements of Statistical Learning (Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman), Section 7.10.2, makes a claim you can reproduce in seconds. Take 50 samples in two equal classes and 5,000 standard-normal predictors that have nothing to do with the labels. Pick the 100 predictors most correlated with the labels using all 50 samples, then estimate a 1-nearest-neighbor classifier's error with cross-validation. The book reports: "Over 50 simulations from this setting, the average CV error rate was 3%." The true error of any classifier here is 50%.

This is the guided capstone. Every milestone below is one your project needs too; if you chose a different target, read each step for its pattern, then fill in the skeleton at the end.

#Milestone 1: The plan, as code

Put the plan's key decisions in variables. Later cells compare results against them, so the notebook can't drift from what you pre-registered.

Two ambiguities, two decisions. The book doesn't say how many folds the 3% used, but its next paragraph describes the samples "as we would do in five-fold cross-validation," so the primary analysis uses 5; 10 is a declared variant. "Highest correlation" could mean signed or absolute; the primary reading is the literal one.

#Milestone 2: The data, with provenance checks

For a simulation, the "dataset" is the generating process, and provenance means checking that it matches the description. Write those checks as asserts so they run every time.

The signal argument is there for a control in Milestone 3. With signal=0 the data are exactly what the book describes.

#Milestone 3: Baseline, controls, and the primary reproduction

The selection step is a vectorized correlation, so all 5,000 predictors are scored in one line. The key switch is select_inside: False is the book's "wrong way" (select once on all samples, then cross-validate), True is the right way (select again inside each training fold).

Read the controls before the headline. The negative control (correct CV on pure noise) lands near 50%, so honest CV on this pipeline doesn't invent signal. The positive control adds a real shift to 10 of the 5,000 predictors, and the same correct CV now finds it, so the pipeline can detect signal when it exists. Only with both in hand does the wrong-way number mean anything: about 4%, from data with no signal at all.

The negative control sits a few points above 50%, which is a known quirk rather than a bug. Holding out a fold of balanced data leaves the training set tilted toward the other class, so a 1-nearest-neighbor classifier leans the wrong way slightly more often than chance.

#Milestone 4: Uncertainty and the verdict

Fifty simulations give fifty CV errors. Their mean has a standard error, and the rule from Milestone 1 compares its 95% interval with the range that rounds to 3%.

The interval only just reaches the rounded range, so the honest verdict is "consistent, with our estimate slightly higher than the book's." Both halves of the qualitative claim reproduce decisively: wrong-way CV reports single-digit error, and correct CV reports roughly 50%.

#Milestone 5: Sensitivity, a secondary claim, and the error distribution

Run the declared variants, exactly the ones listed in the plan, and nothing chosen after the fact.

The fold count barely matters. The reading of "highest correlation" does: selecting by absolute correlation cuts the wrong-way error to about a third, well below the claimed 3%. So the ambiguity is real, and the two readings bracket the book's number.

The book offers a way to break the tie. Its Figure 7.10 takes the 100 predictors chosen on all 50 samples, recomputes their correlations with the labels on 10 random samples, and reports that they "average about 0.28, rather than 0." Under absolute selection, roughly half the chosen predictors correlate negatively, so their average should sit near 0. Check both, pooling one random subset from each of 50 datasets:

The signed reading produces a histogram centered well above zero, like the book's; the absolute reading centers on zero. That supports the primary reading, and you found it in the source, not by tuning toward the number. Our average is somewhat higher than "about 0.28", which is worth one line in the discrepancy log, not a new analysis.

The left panel is the error analysis. Wrong-way errors aren't just low on average; they're low in every simulation, so the optimism is systematic, not an unlucky draw. The right-way errors scatter widely around 50%, which is what honest uncertainty looks like with only 10 test samples per fold.

#Milestone 6: Tests, then the report

Tests turn your claims about the notebook into checks the notebook runs on itself. If someone changes a seed or a library update changes a result, the next "Run all" fails here instead of silently producing a different report.

In Colab, finish with Runtime › Restart session and run all. If every cell runs and the checks pass, the notebook is your reproducibility statement. Commit it with the requirements.txt from Module 1.

#Your own project: the starter skeleton

Copy this into a new notebook. It runs as is on a placeholder target (LDA on the wine data, from Module 7) so you can see every piece work, then replace each marked section with your own.

The shuffled-label control should score near chance (about 1/3 for three classes). If your own version of that line ever scores well above chance, stop and find the leak before doing anything else.

Key takeaways

  • Store the claim, rule, ambiguity decisions, and variants as variables; the notebook checks itself against what you pre-registered.
  • A negative control (no signal) and a positive control (planted signal) prove the pipeline can tell the difference before you trust the headline.
  • Run exactly the declared variants. When they disagree, look for clues in the source itself, like a secondary figure, rather than picking the closest number.
  • End with assert-based tests and a generated summary, then restart and run all.

#Ideas for going further

  • Vary p (500, 5,000, 50,000) and the number kept (10, 100, 1,000). Where does the wrong-way error approach 50%, and why?
  • Reproduce the book's companion point: with correct CV, plot the distribution of selected predictors' correlations on held-out samples (the lower panel of Figure 7.10) and show it centers near 0.
  • Swap 1-nearest-neighbor for logistic regression. Is the optimism a property of the classifier or of the selection step?

m8-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Add reusable tests for group separation, determinism, and controls, and run the notebook the way a reviewer will.
  • Check figures automatically for missing labels, truncated bars, and missing intervals.
  • Structure the written report and a five-minute talk around the claim, the verdict, and the figure that supports it.
  • Assess the study against the rubric, reflect on what you'd change, and pick a place to share it.

A careful reviewer spends the first five minutes with your study doing three things: restarting the notebook and running every cell, finding the one sentence that states the verdict, and looking hard at the main figure. If the notebook fails, the verdict is vague, or the figure exaggerates, they stop trusting everything else. This lesson makes sure all three survive.

#Test the notebook the way a reviewer would

Most notebook bugs that change results come from three places: rows from one group leaking across a split, randomness that isn't pinned, and controls nobody looked at. Write a check for each and put them in a final "tests" section.

The KFold failure is the point: this helper catches the leak from Module 6 the moment someone swaps a splitter. Call check_deterministic on your primary analysis function, and assert that your shuffled-label or negative control sits near chance, as in the previous lesson. Print the library versions at the end so the report can quote them.

Then do the reviewer's run yourself. In Colab: Runtime › Restart session and run all. Better still, open the notebook from a fresh copy of your repository in a new browser profile or on a friend's account, so nothing on your Drive or in memory can quietly help it. Fix whatever breaks, and repeat until a clean run finishes with every test passing.

#Lint your figures

You can check the most common figure problems the same way you check code. This function inspects a matplotlib axis and lists what a reviewer would object to:

A lint pass doesn't make a figure good, but it catches the mistakes that make a figure misleading. Run it on every figure in the report. Then do the human checks it can't: units on every axis, colors that still differ in grayscale and for color-blind readers, compared conditions on one shared axis, and a caption that states the takeaway in words.

#Structure the report around the verdict

A reproduction report is easier to read than a methods paper because it has one question. Put the answer first.

Section What it contains
Abstract (150 words) The claim, what you did, the verdict with numbers and intervals, the main discrepancy.
1. The claim and its context What the paper found, why it matters, where exactly the number appears.
2. Plan The pre-registered rule, primary analysis, ambiguities, and declared variants, dated.
3. Data and provenance Source, version, checks against documentation, anything that couldn't be matched.
4. Methods Checkable detail: splitter, groups, seeds, preprocessing location, library versions.
5. Results Baseline, controls, the primary result with intervals, the claimed-vs-reproduced figure.
6. Sensitivity, ablation, and error analysis Every declared variant, reported whether it helped or not.
7. Discrepancy log Every difference from the paper and what you did about it.
8. Limitations Specific threats and their likely direction.
9. Reproducibility statement Repository link, how to run, environment, and the filled REFORMS checklist.

The abstract's verdict sentence is the most important line you'll write. Compare "We attempted to reproduce the results and found some differences" with "Two of three accuracies reproduced exactly; the third was one wine lower (95.5% vs 96.1%, 95% CI 91.4% to 97.7%), consistent within sampling error." The second can be checked, quoted, and cited.

#Present it in five minutes

Five minutes is enough for one claim and one figure. A workable plan:

  1. The claim (30 seconds). Quote it and say why someone would care if it were wrong.
  2. What you did (45 seconds). Data, method, and the rule you set before running.
  3. The figure (60 seconds). Claimed vs reproduced, with intervals. Point at what the reader should see.
  4. What differed (60 seconds). The biggest discrepancy, what you tested, and what you found.
  5. What it means (45 seconds). The verdict and the most important limitation.
  6. One takeaway (30 seconds). The sentence you want people to remember, plus the repository link.

Rehearse with a timer, out loud, at least twice. Cut slides until you finish with 20 seconds to spare.

#Rubric

Criterion Points Excellent Needs work
Claim and plan 15 Specific quoted claim; dated plan with match rule, ambiguities, and declared variants written before the primary run Vague target, or rule chosen after seeing results
Data provenance 10 Checks against documentation as assertions; unresolvable differences stated Data loaded without any checks
Primary reproduction, baseline, controls 20 Faithful primary analysis; baseline plus a negative (shuffled or null) control, and a positive control where possible No baseline or controls; primary analysis swapped for a better-matching variant
Uncertainty 15 Intervals on every reported number and on the claimed-vs-reproduced comparison; resolution discussed Single numbers without intervals
Sensitivity, ablation, leakage, errors 15 All declared variants reported; leakage risks checked; errors examined, not just counted Variants selectively reported or missing
Reproducible notebook 10 Clean restart-and-run-all; tests pass; versions recorded; public repository Fails on a fresh run or depends on local files
Report and figures 10 Verdict sentence with numbers; checkable methods; specific limitations; figures pass lint; REFORMS attached Missing sections or misleading figures
Talk 5 Five minutes, one figure, clear verdict and limitation Over time or no clear verdict

A study that doesn't reproduce its target can earn full marks. The rubric rewards how well you tested the claim, not whether the paper turned out to be right.

#Reflect

Write a short paragraph on each before you submit. They make good material for the report's limitations section and for your own next project.

  • Which decision in your plan would you change if you started over, and why didn't you see it at the start?
  • Where did the paper's description leave you guessing? Write the sentence the authors should have included.
  • If your result matched, what's the strongest remaining reason it might still be wrong? If it didn't, what's the most likely explanation you couldn't test?
  • Which check from Modules 5 to 7 caught the most problems in your own work?

#Share it and keep going

  • Put it online with a citation. Push the notebook, requirements.txt, report, and checklist to a public GitHub repository. GitHub's guide to referencing and citing content (opens in a new tab) shows how to archive a release on Zenodo and get a DOI so others can cite it.
  • Submit it. ReScience C (opens in a new tab) is a peer-reviewed open-access journal for replications of computational research. The ML Reproducibility Challenge (opens in a new tab) is an annual event that publishes reproductions of recent machine-learning papers.
  • Tell the authors. A short, polite email with your report is useful to them whether you matched or not, and an exact reproduction is good news worth sharing.
  • Read further. The Turing Way (opens in a new tab) covers reproducible research practices well beyond ML, and the REFORMS guidelines (opens in a new tab) explain the reasoning behind every checklist item.

Key takeaways

  • Write tests for group separation, determinism, and controls, then restart and run all from a clean copy until everything passes.
  • Lint every figure for labels, zero-based bars, and intervals, then check what code can't: units, color, captions.
  • Lead the report and the talk with a checkable verdict sentence, then show the one figure that supports it.
  • The rubric rewards how carefully you tested the claim; a well-documented failure to reproduce is a full-credit result.
